Validated across two real-world clinical cohorts, our framework matches state-of-the-art predictive performance while resolving distributional outputs into interpretable risk markers across flexible prognostic horizons.

entries.title: Hierarchical Multi-Channel Tip-Over Prediction via Isolated Temporal Models for Planetary Rover Safety
entries.abstract: Reliable tip-over prevention is critical for planetary rovers operating in unstructured environments where communication delays prevent real-time human intervention. Existing learning-based approaches typically optimize a single prediction objective, limiting their ability to capture both gradual instability evolution and abrupt terrain disturbances. This work presents a hierarchical multi-channel tip-over prediction framework based on isolated temporal learning. A multi-horizon Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) learns progressive instability patterns from inertial measurements, while a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)-based forward dynamics model predicts nominal rover motion and detects unexpected dynamic deviations through prediction residuals. These complementary signals are integrated through decision-level fusion and priority-based arbitration to generate graded safety actions, including early warning and emergency braking. The proposed system is deployed as an Orocos Real-Time Toolkit (RTT)-based safety component within the Rock robotics framework, operating at 100 Hz on a planetary rover software stack. Experiments on Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) samples collected across heterogeneous terrains demonstrate 97.58% event prediction coverage with a 1.82s median lead time, outperforming individual prediction channels. The results validate that isolated temporal models combined through hierarchical decision fusion provide a robust solution for real-time rover safety in uncertain terrain.

entries.title: RAIL: Representation-Aligned Imitation Learning for Student-Compatible Teacher Policies
entries.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) from raw sensory inputs such as images or onboard sensors can be challenging due to high-dimensional observations and sparse rewards. A common strategy is to train a teacher policy with access to privileged state information and then distill it into a student policy that acts from raw inputs alone. However, when the teacher relies on information unavailable to the student, exact imitation may be impossible, creating an irreducible imitation gap. Existing approaches typically mitigate this mismatch through careful reward shaping or additional reinforcement learning on the student policy after the teacher has been trained. Instead, we introduce Representation-Aligned Imitation Learning (RAIL), which addresses the mismatch during teacher training itself. RAIL learns a latent representation shared across teacher and student observations using contrastive learning, and trains the teacher policy directly in this space. Because the teacher policy is constrained to operate on this shared space, it learns behaviors that are reproducible from student observations. This substantially reduces the imitation gap while preserving task performance. Across multiple environments, RAIL outperforms strong baselines without reward modification or post-hoc student fine-tuning, and surpasses direct reinforcement learning from raw observations. The learned representations further enable zero-shot transfer to new tasks through teacher-only training. Project site: https://merajmammadov.com/rail/.

entries.title: A method to automatically discover symbolic local learning rules
entries.abstract: We present a general method for discovering symbolic local learning rules that can replace backpropagation, applicable, in principle, to any deep learning architecture and task. The method automatically discovers local loss functions specific to each layer by (1) constructing a dictionary of monomials of local tensor variables, inspired by Penrose diagram notation, (2) regressing over coefficients weighting these monomials to build layerwise polynomial losses whose gradients together minimize a target global loss. We test the method on classification, reconstruction, and self-supervised learning tasks with small multilayer networks and minimal datasets. Across all tasks, the discovered rules induce non-trivial interactions between layers, which lead to significant reductions in the corresponding global losses. Furthermore, the method selects sparse combinations of monomials, finding local rules that are more interpretable than those generated by MLP-based alternatives. The potential implications of our method range from energy-efficient deep learning to the discovery of biologically plausible learning mechanisms.

entries.title: CADMA: Capacity-Aware Coverage Decomposition for Generative Model Assessment
entries.abstract: Evaluating generative models requires measuring not only sample fidelity but also how well a generated set covers the real data distribution. Recent work has therefore introduced recall-oriented metrics for distribution-level evaluation. However, existing recall metrics often reduce distributional coverage to geometry-based coverage. This simplifying assumption weakens their diagnostic value and interpretability in two ways: these metrics provide only a single aggregate score that cannot distinguish essential diversity failures such as mode dropping and mode collapse, and geometry-based coverage can provide unreliable estimates by assigning high scores to poorly covered generative distributions. We therefore introduce CADMA, a capacity-aware framework for recall-oriented evaluation and diagnosis. CADMA evaluates distributional coverage through local capacity matching between real and generated samples, separating geometry-based coverage from effective coverage. This yields multi-dimensional coverage diagnostics that quantify mode dropping and mode collapse while reducing the overly optimistic estimates produced by geometry-based metrics. Through extensive experiments on toy data, real-world datasets, and generative models, we show that CADMA provides more reliable coverage estimates and more fine-grained, interpretable diagnostic signals of diversity failures than existing metrics. Our code is available at https://github.com/Open-Debin/CADMA_NeurIPS2026.

entries.title: Controlling Temporal Pseudo-Label Marginals for Stable Online Test-Time Adaptation
entries.abstract: Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) methods update models online using a stream of unlabeled data to overcome distribution shifts encountered at test time. However, CTTA is often unstable, as it can reinforce biases in early predictions and increasingly predict only a few classes, resulting in drift or even collapse. In this paper, we identify narrowing pseudo-label class usage as an indicator of CTTA instability and quantify this behavior. Most existing methods have attempted to address this issue by either selecting reliable adaptation samples or re-weighting the loss to encourage diverse pseudo-labels, but they do not explicitly enforce a class marginal over a temporal window. Instead, we propose Sinkhorn Class-Marginal Regularization (SCALAR), a simple plug-and-play module that controls the pseudo-label distribution over a short temporal window. SCALAR works by maintaining recent predictions in a buffer, balancing their class distribution via the Sinkhorn algorithm to match a specified target distribution, and using the balanced soft targets for adaptation. Without changing the model architecture, SCALAR maintains the per-step runtime and increases the peak allocated GPU memory by only 10 MB on ImageNet-C. Our method is particularly effective on skewed, non-stationary data with severe distribution shifts, where SCALAR significantly alleviates drift and collapse when combined with existing stabilization methods based on entropy or diversity.
entries.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 20 pages. Code: https://github.com/r-isr/SCALAR

entries.title: Prune, Don't Merge: Expert Compression of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs on Multilingual Production Tasks
entries.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts language models are cheap to run per token but expensive to hold in GPU memory, which drives the cost of serving them in production. One-shot expert compression shrinks them after a single calibration pass. Its two current state-of-the-art methods are REAP for expert pruning, which deletes the least salient experts, and REAM for expert merging, which merges them into the most salient ones. Both have been evaluated only on academic benchmarks. We compare the two on five multilingual production tasks of a web-hosting company, from classification to the generation of marketing HTML email templates, with two 30B-parameter models (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and the hybrid Mamba-attention Nemotron-3.5-Lightning) at 25% and 50% of experts removed and the same calibration data. Pruning wins: on the same rows, REAP is significantly better in 16 of 20 comparisons and REAM in 2. At 25%, REAP keeps 93.6% of Qwen3-30B's generative quality and REAM 62.5%, although on benchmarks the two are within a point for the same model. The damage concentrates in the output contract rather than the content: 89.8-95.2% of each significant loss on email templates comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts and runaway generation, and most failed non-English domain descriptions copy the prompt's English opening phrase. Cross-perplexity and logit divergence, two diagnostics from the REAP paper, also track production quality, as does the rate of repetition loops; n-gram diversity does not. We close with practical guidance for compressing MoE models for production.

entries.title: A Cost That Practice Accuracy Hides: Worked Solutions in Self-Generated Training Data and the Compositional Use of New Rules
entries.abstract: A worked solution can make self-generated training targets shorter and cheaper, but accuracy on the practiced operation may hide how well a model can reuse newly learned rules. We study this choice in a 2B-parameter reasoning model learning two invented quantitative rules. The model generates targets from a rule sheet alone or from the sheet plus a program-written worked solution; targets are accepted for final-answer correctness, and the support is removed for fine-tuning and evaluation. Training questions request forward use in one segment; composition requires sequential reuse of the same rule across two segments. After six passes, using a program-checked numerical signature, sheet-only targets lead by 24.3 percentage points (95% item-bootstrap CI 14.6-34.0) on composition in a prospective test. On unseen argument values, observed forward accuracy is identical (87.5% each), but composition accuracy is 58.3% versus 23.6%, a 34.7-point gap (25.7-43.8). An independently sampled second target-bank pair repeats the direction (+14.6 points, 2.1-26.0). Ten passes on the shorter worked-solution targets, approximately matching the domain tokens of six sheet-only passes while changing other training quantities, narrow the gap to 16.3 points (6.3-26.7) in the first bank pair and 6.2 points (-6.3 to 18.8) in the second, where the pre-specified test does not hold. At six passes each, the worked-solution policy uses fewer capture tokens and less update time, yet the trained models use 2.6 times as many generated tokens per composition success under the numerical signature (2.1 times in the second bank pair). Choosing a capture context therefore requires testing how the new rules are reused, alongside the inference cost of those uses, rather than relying on forward accuracy alone.
entries.comment: 31 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables. Code, data and trained adapters: https://github.com/JetXu-LLM/kestrel-capture-context

entries.title: An Empirical Evaluation of Quantum Kernel Stability in Network Intrusion Detection
entries.abstract: Quantum kernel methods have been proposed for network intrusion detection, yet their performance limitations are often attributed to noise in current quantum hardware. This study evaluates that assumption through a controlled analysis of Pegasos-QSVC on the NSL-KDD and ToN-IoT datasets. We perform 56 quantum experiments using one exact noiseless statevector backend and three noise-simulated superconducting backends while keeping preprocessing, PCA features, data splits, and classical baselines identical. XGBoost achieves accuracies of 98.94% on NSL-KDD and 99.41% on ToN-IoT, compared with 91.80% and 82.98% for Pegasos-QSVC. The quantum model also exhibits substantially greater seed-dependent variability. Eight runs collapse into degenerate classifiers, including four recall-collapse cases and four trivial-positive classifiers. Notably, two failures occur on the noiseless backend, demonstrating that hardware noise is not a necessary condition for classi-fier collapse. Kernel Gram matrix analysis further reveals low effective rank and severe ill-conditioning even in the absence of noise, indicating intrinsic fragility in the learned quantum representation. These results show that average accuracy alone can conceal operationally unacceptable behavior and highlight the importance of reporting worst-case performance, seed-level variability, class-specific metrics, and explicit degeneracy tests in quantum intrusion detection studies.

entries.title: A Geometric Invariant of Attention Predicts Head Specialization from Weights Alone
entries.abstract: Transformers are built with continuous symmetries in the attention mechanism. We derive ρ, a scalar invariant that measures each head's capacity to couple to rotary positional encodings. This framework allows us to analyze heads without forward passes, opening a new research direction into data-independent analysis of modern LLMs. Empirically, we find that ρ predicts induction heads, the most-studied circuit type in mechanistic interpretability, with Spearman correlation between -0.55 and -0.74 across four bias-free RoPE models spanning 135M to 7B parameters. As a preliminary proof of concept, we use ρ to apply YaRN to only the top-50% positional heads, which degrades perplexity less than uniform application. Code is available at https://github.com/MPedraBento/rho-invariant.
entries.comment: Accepted as an extended abstract at the Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations Workshop (NeurReps), NeurIPS 2026

entries.title: Harnessing Vision-Language Models for Federated Unsupervised Visual Recognition
entries.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a promising research paradigm that enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without data sharing. To handle unlabeled data in local clients, existing unsupervised FL research has primarily focused on tasks like clustering and self-supervised representation learning, leaving the critical problem of unsupervised visual recognition largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce FedUR, the first framework designed for unsupervised recognition by leveraging the zero-shot capabilities of pre-trained vision-language models like CLIP. Specifically, FedUR addresses data heterogeneity through a pseudo-labeling mechanism with a class-aware data selection strategy. This strategy first estimates a global pseudo-label distribution, then allocates pseudo-labeled data to clients accordingly. To handle the uncertainty of conventional positive pseudo-labels, FedUR further incorporates class weights and a negative pseudo-labeling strategy. Furthermore, FedUR proposes a personalized prompt aggregation protocol where general visual prompts are aggregated on the server, and personalized text prompts encoding local knowledge are retained on clients. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedUR consistently outperforms baseline methods under both label-level and feature-level distribution shifts. We believe this work paves the way for further advances in federated unsupervised recognition. Code will be available at github.com/tim-learn/FedUR/.

entries.title: NearFormer: Linear-Size Sparse Attention via Randomized Near Neighbors
entries.abstract: Graph transformers can capture long-range interactions, but their quadratic attention cost limits their use on large graphs. We introduce NearFormer, a graph transformer whose global attention is restricted to a randomized near-neighbor (NN) graph. NearFormer uses an efficient randomized construction to connect each node to a small number of near neighbors from a broader neighborhood defined by a label-independent feature or spectral geometry. For a fixed retained budget k, the resulting attention support has linear size O(|E|+nk). The NN graph is built once by within-bin search and then held fixed. We use these edges as sparse global-attention supports, with optional learned attention biases, while preserving the original graph for local message passing. Experiments on long-range graph benchmarks and synthetic structural tasks show that NearFormer provides a favorable accuracy–scalability trade-off relative to local message passing, dense and sparse attention.

entries.title: Replication of Thermal Comfort Cohort Models: No Support for Improved Thermal Preference Prediction
entries.abstract: Cohort comfort models (CCMs) aim to overcome the extensive individual data requirements of personal comfort models (PCMs) by grouping occupants based on demographic and psychometric characteristics (cold start) or similar thermal preferences (warm start). We evaluated the validity of the reported CCM performance gains through (i) a methodological assessment of the original study, (ii) a replication using one of the two original datasets (DORN: 20 participants, 6 months) under a revised experimental protocol, and (iii) a replication using an independently collected dataset (PersonAI: 72 participants, 4 weeks). Classification performance was evaluated using F1-micro, as in the original study, and F1-macro to account for class imbalance. Under F1-micro, a trivial baseline that always outputs the majority class performed on par with cohort models. Under F1-macro, all cohort models achieved lower median scores than a simple baseline that makes random predictions based on the estimated distribution of thermal preferences. In our methodological assessment we identified the following key issues: Limited data per participant and per minority class, reliance on a metric insensitive to class imbalance, missing trivial baselines, inadequate cross validation strategy, and multiple occurrences of information leakage. Our findings challenge the original study's conclusion that CCMs improve thermal preference prediction. CCMs did not outperform simple class-distribution baselines. Future studies should improve experimental designs, including controlled thermal conditions, to obtain sufficient observations across thermal preference classes.

entries.title: FraudBench: A Legal Evaluation of AI Deception
entries.abstract: We introduce FraudBench, an evaluation of large language models' (LLMs) propensities to recommend, assist, or directly take actions that would constitute fraud under U.S. law. Our evaluation contains a novel dataset of 159 scenarios based on real-world U.S. court cases and validated by legal experts. We present each scenario to LLMs via three tasks at varying levels of autonomy: advising users, drafting messages for users to send, and acting directly on behalf of users (477 tasks total). In each scenario, FraudBench re-enacts the facts of a court case to give LLMs an opportunity, but no explicit instruction, to either misrepresent or conceal a material fact in a high-stakes commercial setting–e.g., whether to describe company-funded product testing as "independent" to customers (misrepresentation) or whether to hide unfavorable regulatory investigations from clients (concealment). We evaluate 20 LLMs across 25 experimental conditions (totaling >300,000 generations) and include a preregistered human baseline (n_annotations = 2,957, n_humans = 996). We score a response as fraudulent when it engages in, assists with, or recommends misrepresentation or concealment. Key findings include: (1) across LLMs, fraud rates ranged from near 0% to over 40%; (2) LLM fraud rates increased with autonomy, with overall rates of 3.0% when advising, 14.7% when drafting, and 21.4% when acting directly, without applying pressure; (3) LLMs sometimes engaged in fraud despite recognizing legal risks; (4) LLMs more often engaged in fraud by concealment than by misrepresentation; and (5) prompt-based interventions substantially affected fraud rates, with a prompt to obey the law reducing fraud rates, while prompts to maximize profits and act agentically increased fraud rates.

entries.title: Same Physics, Different Gradients: A State-of-the-Art Report on Differentiable Physics Simulation
entries.abstract: Differentiable simulation propagates derivatives through a physics simulator, turning animation, system identification, control, and computational design into gradient-based optimization. Engines differ in the physics they model and, less visibly, in which mathematical object they differentiate. We separate two questions the literature conflates. The referent is which object the returned derivative belongs to: the finite computation that executed, the converged equation it approximates, or the continuous dynamics. The realization describes the organization of the backward pass: automatically generated differentiation, an equation-level adjoint solve, or a custom adjoint. The referent defines the target against which exactness is assessed; the implementation determines how accurately that target is approximated. Cost depends on the realization together with how the states needed by the backward pass are retained or recovered. Crossing the axes places every method and engine we classify in a cell, separates claims the literature merges, and shows that the apparent trade-off between exactness and memory follows from how methods have been built rather than from a constraint. A second, orthogonal taxonomy covers contact, where the map is non-smooth. We then ask whether a correct gradient helps. Four mechanisms by which useful gradients are lost are cataloged and measured on one testbed, where the advantage of the exact derivative over the equation-level adjoint depends on where the fitting target comes from as much as on the solver budget, and we review the evidence that zeroth-order methods can outperform simulator gradients in the regimes where those mechanisms act. The model classes, systems techniques and applications are surveyed through this lens, and we close with a reporting checklist, a released diagnostic that computes it, and a research agenda.

entries.title: GPU-Accelerated Non-Interactive Encrypted Neural Network Training with Batched Diagonal Packing
entries.abstract: Training a neural network under homomorphic encryption requires transposes, batch reductions, optimizer updates, and repeated refreshes in addition to forward matrix products. We combine rectangular diagonal packing, feature-major SIMD mini-batch lanes, baby-step giant-step evaluation, and compact optimizer state in an MIT-licensed Rust CKKS implementation. Its CUDA path keeps training and bootstrap ciphertext arithmetic on the GPU, while retaining host key generation and client operations. In a matched 100-update experiment on the main non-interactive MNIST model, device-resident bootstrapping reduces training time from 14,268.295 to 293.075 seconds, a 48.68× ratio against our CPU implementation, with exactly equal decoded parameters and predictions. Including setup and final evaluation gives a 40.67× ratio. A separate GPU run completes ten passes over 4,800 images in 2,967.095 seconds and achieves 90.35% test accuracy versus 90.41% for its plaintext twin. These are single-initialization results; exact CPU/GPU parameter agreement is verified at 100 updates, not for the full 1,000-update run. Earlier completed CPU runs support a larger-batch key-switch advantage and baseline-batch accuracy within the registered tolerance, but the baseline-batch normalized key-switch target is missed. The released ReBoot baseline does not meet the common security-estimator threshold, and its full-setting CPU time is unmeasured. We therefore distinguish measured acceleration of our implementation from conditional layout comparisons and do not claim unconditional superiority over ReBoot.
entries.comment: 12 pages. Research preprint. Code and evidence: https://github.com/kenmaro3/ckks-train

entries.title: Beyond Flat Walks: Compositional Abstraction for Autoregressive Graph Generation
entries.abstract: Autoregressive graph generators typically linearize graphs through flat node-edge walks, which can obscure higher-order structure in large and complex graphs. We introduce a hierarchical graph abstraction and coarse-to-fine generation pipeline that separates coarsening, tokenization, and decoding. This exposes three design axes: community coarsening, hierarchical tokenization, and order randomization. Across these axes, traversal-based hierarchy consistently improves distributional and structural fidelity, while its V.U.N. cost depends strongly on the coarsening and randomization policy. In particular, the fidelity–V.U.N. trade-off observed under within-community randomization is substantially reduced when traversal order is randomized across the full hierarchy. With a fixed backbone, training protocol, and matched training time across five molecular and five non-molecular benchmarks, hierarchical serialization yields consistent distributional and structural gains on all molecular datasets, while the non-molecular results further show that these gains depend on how well the supplied hierarchy aligns with structure in the target distribution. Together, these results characterize when and how hierarchical serialization benefits autoregressive graph generation.

entries.title: The balance between feature learning and collapse in dynamical systems-based generative models
entries.abstract: Over the past decade, a growing body of work has established that implicit biases in learning dynamics fundamentally shape the solutions found by neural networks, governing their learned features and generalisation performance. However, despite these strides in deep learning theory, far less is known about representation learning in generative models based on dynamical systems, from normalising flows to diffusion. Importantly, empirical evidence suggests that continuous-time generative models can be prone to mode collapse, yet a learning theory explaining such biases remains elusive. To address this, we use tools from dynamical systems and operator theory to express the gradient flow of a general class of stochastic differential equations as a composition of linear operators, allowing us to relate collapse to low-rank biases in generative models. In variational inference and flow-matching tasks, we show that this bias can manifest in two different mechanisms: i) where collapsed models are stable fixed points of the gradient flow, or ii) in sequential feature learning, where smaller modes take progressively longer to be learned, producing an effective collapse for a fixed training budget. Together these findings point to a trade-off between feature learning and collapse, suggesting an operator view as a step towards a unified framework for understanding the learning dynamics of dynamical systems-based generative models.

entries.title: Do Time-Series Foundation Models Forecast Index-Futures Returns? A Preregistered Evaluation of Models, Metrics, and Input Representations
entries.abstract: We ask whether the apparent forecasting skill of frozen time-series foundation models (TSFMs) on intraday index-futures returns is incremental skill. In a pre-registered evaluation on E-mini Nasdaq-100 (NQ) and E-mini S&P 500 (ES) futures, a common panel of five zero-shot models (Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5, Moirai 2.0 and TiRex), plus separate experiments with Kronos, is compared with a no-change forecast at 5-120 minutes, using native prices, log returns, volatility-standardised returns and a volume clock as inputs. On a blind set opened once, 0 of 160 model-representation-horizon-market cells beat no-change, and a Hansen SPA test gives p = 1.000 on both markets; a later retrospective hold-out, scored as a descriptive check, gives 0 of 120. Input representations change forecast magnitude but not accuracy, and a transformation-aware ridge regression does as well. Several standard measures nevertheless suggest skill. Price-level correlation exceeds 0.9996, but no-change scores higher. Within-day RankIC across forecast origins rewards a trivial revert-to-mean rule (+0.35 at 30 minutes); we derive the expected within-day covariance under a random walk in closed form, and a sign-randomised null reproduces about 95% of the observed value. One model beats HAR for 5-minute volatility, but not the EWMA its input already contains. On strongly planted synthetic signals the models recover part of the signal at 5 minutes, and recovery deteriorates at 30 minutes. Benchmark-level success of TSFMs should therefore not be assumed to carry over to low-signal domains such as intraday returns.

entries.title: Visible Tails: Characterizing Adaptation to Unknown Moments in Heavy-Tailed Bandits
entries.abstract: Heavy-tailed bandit learners must tell a poor arm from an arm whose favorable rewards have not yet appeared. We characterize this obstruction through a scale of one-sided visibility conditions on the optimal reward law: the mean hidden in a rare event is at most a constant multiple of a retained central moment. A quantile-trimmed UCB index that is given the visibility constants attains arm-specific moment rates at every exponent, with no lower bound on the exponent. Conversely, every strategy with a fixed exploration budget has polynomial regret on each law that violates the corresponding condition. For the variance benchmark we determine the order of both budget constants in the visibility level. The frontier depends on the largest exponent the benchmark promises, and the resulting classes are strictly nested. The same index has logarithmic expected regret when rewards are integrable, with a coefficient that can be exponential in the inverse gap.

entries.title: Good Views Are Not Enough: Global Counterexamples for Gaussian-Regularized JEPAs
entries.abstract: Good views do not suffice to guarantee scene invariance or uniqueness up to rotation at the global optima of Gaussian-regularized JEPAs. We give globally certified counterexamples showing that the uniqueness premise of the Gaussian extension in Good Views fails for specified soft objectives. Gaussian marginal matching can reward retaining independently resampled observation variation, and this benefit can exceed its prediction cost. In a four-state model, comparison against the entire scene-only class proves that every global minimizer splits a scene and admits an equal-value partner outside its rotation orbit. In a 512-dimensional model with a complete scene basis, a spectral gap, and exact population whitening, pooled Epps-Pulley regularization still forces every global minimizer to retain nuisance and yields positive cross-modal alignment error even after the best rotation when modality nuisances are independent. Better scene alignment can also accompany worse prediction. With matched 512-label readout budgets and 1% observation noise, whitened prediction JEPA aligns better to the scene than next-token prediction but incurs 0.2872 nats/token higher linear-readout test NLL. A Bayes-risk decomposition distinguishes information lost through the observation channel from the fitted readout's difficulty using retained information. These results connect three determinants of learned representations: what views share, what regularization favors, and what a prediction task can use.

entries.title: One-Shot Federated Graph Learning via High-Fidelity Proxies and Transferability-Guided Collaboration
entries.abstract: One-shot Federated Graph Learning (OFGL) has emerged as a communication-efficient paradigm for federated graph learning under strict bandwidth constraints, compressing collaboration into a single transmission round. Nevertheless, this extreme setting suffers from a fundamental Single-Transmission Bottleneck, which limits both the quality and utility of exchanged knowledge. First, while existing methods attempt to distill private graphs into shareable proxies, their aggressive one-shot compression inherently triggers a fidelity crisis. This compression distorts local graph topology and semantics across clients, leading to externalized knowledge underexpression. Second, although the server aggregates these proxies to update global models, current integration schemes suffer from transferability agnosticism. The server cannot reliably identify cross-client collaboration potential, thus resulting in integrated knowledge underutilization. To tackle these dual challenges, we propose FedHFT, an effective One-Shot Personalized Federated Graph Learning (OPFGL) framework that addresses this bottleneck from two perspectives, namely High-Fidelity Knowledge Externalization and Transferability-Ware Knowledge Integration. We use Fidelity-Driven Proxy Refinement to preserve client-side knowledge fidelity, and Transferability-Steered Personalized Collaboration to enable adaptive server-side collaboration. The superiority of FedHFT is validated through extensive experiments on both homophilic and heterophilic graphs. The code is available at https://github.com/Jumpy-Juice/FedHFT.

entries.title: CARE-PO: Controllable Tool-Call Efficiency for LLM Agents
entries.abstract: External tool calls are a major running cost of an LLM agent, while its training objectives align almost exclusively with task completion. In a step-level diagnosis of Qwen3.5 trajectories at two model sizes on GAIA, a long-horizon tool-use benchmark, we find that most contain removable calls, at a similar rate at both sizes. Some methods add an efficiency reward to the objective to reduce the call count, but introduce problems of their own: the anchor they price calls against is computed from the policy's own rollouts (e.g., the group's shortest correct rollout) and so moves with the policy; training can drift toward a collapsed policy that issues no tool call at all, a degeneracy seen in published reports and in our 27B baseline; and a training run delivers a single operating point, so the user cannot trade efficiency against capability. We present CARE-PO (Controllable Anchored Relative Efficiency Policy Optimization) to mitigate these problems. The efficiency reward prices calls against a reference budget anchored to the task's own difficulty and fixed before training. Injecting a successful trajectory from the training data into each online GRPO rollout group and charging for evidence a trajectory never gathers ease the drift toward a collapsed call count. Shaping the cost curve by an effort tag in the prompt yields an efficiency and a capability operating point from a single training run. On GAIA, five of the six operating points across three model sizes improve on their base model in success rate and call count at once. On four held-out multi-hop benchmarks the result is size-dependent: at 27B and 4B success rate is held or raised at a lower call count, while at 9B both operating points trade success rate for fewer calls. The call count remains well above zero throughout training at all three sizes.

entries.title: Forecast Value Add: Reward-Based Action Selection over Probabilistic Demand Forecasts
entries.abstract: Strong machine-learning ensembles capture much of the trend, seasonality, and known events in demand, yet they can still understate peaks, miss moving events, or mistake temporary changes for shifts in demand level. We address this gap by framing forecast refinement as a reward-driven decision problem. For each forecast period, we let an agent choose among values already produced by the ensemble: its base forecast, distribution-free bounds, quantiles, and a bias-corrected estimate. We evaluate these choices against context-matched historical periods, accounting for calendar position, recurring and moving events, trend, price, and promotions. We then apply a structural seasonal guard to constrain adjustments and record the model, agent, and planner contributions to every published value. We evaluate our approach across five retail, consumer-goods, and direct-to-consumer deployments over nine months. Our refined forecasts reduce mean WMAPE by 6.3% compared with the stacked machine-learning forecast for every customer, with gains reaching 16.7%, and achieve the lowest error in 35 of 45 customer-months. Compared with statistical forecasts, our approach reduces mean error by 18.7%. These results demonstrate that context-aware, auditable action selection can add forecast value beyond a strong ensemble.

entries.title: SkillDuet: Co-Evolving Models and Skills through Response Feedback
entries.abstract: During reinforcement learning, experience can be both internalized in LLM parameters and retained externally as reusable textual skills. Parameter updates alter the model's behavior and the interaction experience from which new skills are extracted. These skills, in turn, guide the model's subsequent interactions and parameter updates. As the model's capabilities evolve, previously beneficial skills may become redundant or detrimental. We present SkillDuet, a framework that coordinates parameter updates and skill evolution through model response feedback. Skills extracted from on-policy trajectories guide parameter updates through OPD at every step. A response-based score, Strength, ranks candidate skills by the magnitude of the shift they induce in the current model's responses, and the highest-scoring skills are periodically consolidated into a persistent global skill set (Global). The updated model and Global jointly guide subsequent interactions, generating experience for further parameter and skill updates. With Qwen3-4B, SkillDuet achieves success rates of 98.57% on ALFWorld and 92.97% on WebShop, exceeding the matched SEED-API baseline by 2.86 and 5.47 percentage points, respectively. Ablations show that response-based skill selection and Global consolidation improve task performance. Further experiments show that the benefits of retained skills depend on both their content and their compatibility with the model. SkillDuet provides a concrete mechanism for model-skill co-evolution and skill-level recursive self-improvement.

entries.title: FALC: An Artifact-Centric Life Cycle Model and Research Agenda for AI Forensics
entries.abstract: AI systems increasingly appear in criminal investigations as tools, targets, and sources of evidence, yet AI forensics lacks a systematic account of the artifacts they produce: investigators often do not know which traces to look for, and for many traces they do find, no established analysis technique exists. In this paper we first developed the Forensic AI Life Cycle (FALC) that unlike other life cycle models shifts the focus onto the forensic artifacts created during the life cycle of an AI system. Through FALC we derived a reference list of artifacts that might serve an investigation. Second, we collected examples for crimes with AI involvement throughout FALC and questions likely to be asked when investigating these crimes. Third, we propose a taxonomy of forensic fields of expertise with a focus on the current possibility to analyze AI forensic artifacts using established techniques. For investigators, the model provides a systematic basis for identifying which artifacts to look for when an AI system is relevant to a case. For researchers, the classification shows where existing forensic methods already suffice and where new techniques are most urgently needed.

entries.title: Calibrating Document-Local Boundaries for Contextual Chunk Retrieval
entries.abstract: Late Chunking encodes an entire document before pooling at chunk boundaries, preserving document context in local retrieval units. Chunk-level post-training improves context-dependent retrieval, but shared context can make semantically similar same-document negatives difficult to distinguish. We study the local decision boundary between a gold chunk and its hardest sibling. Starting from InSeNT, we analyze InSeNT's within-document gradients and show that the entropy of the conditional negative allocation decreases monotonically with the scaling factor at fixed logits. We propose a two-part framework for calibrating document-local chunk boundaries. The first component adapts the discriminative scale from within-document margins, while the second exposes chunk partitions to attention during document encoding. Experiments on ConTEB and NanoBEIR show that the resulting model improves contextual chunk retrieval across the evaluated encoder settings while retaining competitive passage-level retrieval quality; ablations further characterize the distinct roles of adaptive scaling and chunk-aware routing.

entries.title: TSFFormer: A Frequency-Domain Spike Transformer for Green Human Activity Recognition
entries.abstract: Wearable Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) enable pervasive Human Activity Recognition (HAR), but traditional Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) suffer from an "arithmetic-latency deadlock" due to dense floating-point MAC operations. While Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer ultra-low power, existing ones face spatial blind spots, rigid neurons, and gradient degradation. To address these, we propose TSFFormer, a purely spiking Fourier Transformer for Green HAR. It introduces two key innovations: (1) a MultiHeadFourier attention that performs frequency-domain global mixing, reducing complexity from O(V²) to O(VlogV), eliminating spatial blind spots, and saving ~50% GPU memory; and (2) a dual-compartment Temporal Spiking LIF (TSLIFNode) that utilizes dynamic thresholds to adapt to non-stationary rhythms and mitigate gradient degradation. Extensive experiments on 8 public IMU benchmarks demonstrate that TSFFormer surpasses state-of-the-art SNNs and even the classic DeepConvLSTM, achieving a ~3× faster training speed with an energy footprint of 0.1 pJ. Ablation studies confirm the synergistic effect of our modules, providing a highly accurate, ultra-low-power event-driven paradigm for wearable sensing.

entries.title: Zero-Search Reinforcement Learning for Slay the Spire 2 with Failure-Driven Restarts
entries.abstract: Slay the Spire 2 (STS2) is a deck-building roguelike in which a winning run at the highest difficulty takes several hundred decisions, and most losses happen in late boss fights that a learner seldom reaches. We train agents that choose every action with one forward pass of a 6.6M-parameter entity transformer, without lookahead. Training and evaluation run the game's own compiled assembly (v0.107.1) in a headless.NET host. The host replays a run exactly from its seed and actions, so training episodes can restart from states the learner has visited, and a failure-driven curriculum allocates these restarts in proportion to where complete runs are lost. On 12,800 held-out games at Ascension 10 (A10), the released policies win 8.05% averaged over the five characters (Ironclad 15.6%, Regent 12.5%), and AlphaSpire's released networks used without search win 0.55% on a common panel. Longer A10 training raised Ironclad from 12.4% to 15.6% and Defect from 3.0% to 8.1% on these games. At Ascension 0 the released policies win 80.2%, level with the 80.3% that the tree-search agent Spire Mentor reports, while Mentor leads by 5 to 8 points from A4 upward. Run in our host on the same 2,000 A10 games, Mentor's search wins 8.8% against 8.2% for our policies, which need 21-27 ms per decision on one CPU core. GPT-6 Astra at maximum reasoning won none of 11 A10 games through our text interface. In a controlled study of 18 training runs from six random initializations, failure-driven allocation exceeds uniform restart allocation on each of three Regent initializations, by 3.6 percentage points on average, while the Silent effect is small and changes sign. Code, trained policies, an in-game mod and the records behind every table are at https://github.com/HalfVulpes/sts2ai.
entries.comment: 21 pages, 4 figures. Code, released policies and an in-game mod: https://github.com/HalfVulpes/sts2ai ; records behind every table: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1OP9IzFIYPuyR97eg1XZru6bpZDSh87Oz

entries.title: Correct First, Fast Second: What a Local 7B Code Model Can and Cannot Do for GPU Kernel Optimization
entries.abstract: We study how much the interaction strategy around a fixed, locally hosted 7B-parameter code model (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct) affects its ability to replace PyTorch operators with custom CUDA kernels. On 30 KernelBench tasks (levels 1-3, first 10 each, evaluated on a V100), we compare four regimes of increasing structure: zero-shot prompting, profiling-guided prompting, iterative refinement on execution feedback, and a multi-agent loop (analysis, retrieval, generation, evaluation, feedback triage) in which the same model fills four roles around a non-LLM evaluator. Three findings stand out. (1) Correctness, not speed, is the binding constraint: even correct generated kernels average 0.97-0.99x the speed of eager PyTorch, because a 7B model cannot out-write cuBLAS/cuDNN on dense GEMM and convolution; the only real wins are fused memory-bound epilogues. (2) The best strategy depends on difficulty: profiling-guided prompting is strongest overall (43% correct, 27% faster than baseline), but the agent loop is the only method that solves any level-2 fusion problem (3/10 vs. 0/10 for all others). (3) Naive agentic scaffolding is actively harmful: our first agent scored 3% correct, below zero-shot's 30%, and the decisive repairs were matching the agent's ambition to the model's competence and spending compute on best-of-n sampling under a real execution oracle (3% to 33% correct from n=1 to n=8), not on more reasoning steps.

entries.title: XposedMIA: Exploiting Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) for One-Shot Membership Inference Attacks
entries.abstract: Machine learning (ML) services increasingly expose explainability outputs alongside model predictions. While such explanations are intended to improve transparency, they may also reveal information about the underlying training data. In this work, we show that the local surrogate geometry employed by Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) can be repurposed as a proxy for a sample's distance to the model's decision boundary. We extend this boundary-distance view to tabular counterfactual explanations and, for the first time, to visual counterfactual explanations for image classifiers. We present XposedMIA, a one-shot, explanation-based black-box membership inference attack (MIA) framework that converts the returned explanation into a proxy for the queried sample's distance to the model decision boundary. After a one-time calibration step on a small labeled calibration set of as few as 30 samples, our attack requires only a single query for each target sample. Unlike prior label-only attacks requiring iterative queries or shadow training, our method relies solely on the predicted label and its accompanying explanation. Our evaluation indicates that XposedMIA achieves high effectiveness, with success rates of up to 0.95 using only a single query per target, revealing that releasing explanations introduces an additional channel for membership leakage.

entries.title: Translating KV Caches Between Hybrid-Attention Language Models: MLA Latents, Linear-Attention States and Sparse-Attention Indexers
entries.abstract: A model that takes over another model's conversation must normally re-read the whole history; a text hand-off shortens the re-read only by dropping content. KV-cache translation instead maps the source's cache into the target's own format, so the target continues from the full context without re-reading it. It works for grouped-query attention (GQA), but open-weights frontier models now cache compressed latents (MLA), sparse-attention indexer keys and fixed-size linear-attention states. We replicate KV-Lingo on a GQA pair and then give, for each of these objects, where to capture and inject it and a mechanism that reaches native quality. We study two hybrid pairs at 16-48B scale in both directions, Kimi-VL-A3B - Kimi-Linear-48B (MLA - MLA + Kimi Delta Attention) and Qwen3.5-27B - Qwen3.8-27B (Gated DeltaNet hybrids), plus a sparse-attention target (Qwen3.8-27B - Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). MLA latents translate with token-wise linear maps; recurrent states are copied with a closed-form correction or synthesised by replaying the target's own recurrence. Exact long-range recall needs token identity: decoding token ids from the source's layer-0 MLA latent raises needle recall from 0.09 to 0.99 at 2-32K and to 0.83-1.00 at 64K, eight times the longest training prompt. The hybrid full-MLA direction is within the paired confidence interval of native quality on every task metric, and same-shape GDN hybrids reach the native level in both directions (apart from 6% refusals inherited from the source), with time to first token 18.7 and 46.8 times shorter than a re-read at 64K tokens. Segment-wise multi-turn transfer stays at the re-prefill level; naive re-translation collapses. On the sparse-attention target, predicted indexer keys recall the needle as well as the target's own keys (one seed). We state as a hypothesis how the recipes transfer to 300B+ hybrid flagships.

entries.title: BARS: Beat-Adaptive Rap Synthesis via Flow Matching
entries.abstract: We present BARS (Beat-Adaptive Rap Synthesis), a non-autoregressive rapping voice generation model based on Flow Matching, conditioned on a beat track (instrumental backing), lyrics, and a short reference voice for zero-shot timbre control. Unlike prior autoregressive rap synthesis, where rap pace and output duration are strictly determined by the beat, BARS enables independent control over the rap tempo, allowing flexible-length generation without explicit duration prediction or phoneme-level alignment. We encode lyrics using a pretrained ByT5 encoder with a lightweight Transformer adapter trained jointly with the model, without relying on speech-pretrained text encoders, enabling natural handling of non-standard orthography (e.g., slang, abbreviations) and numerals common in rap lyrics. To address alignment instabilities, such as token skipping or repetition, under strong beat conditioning, we propose Asymmetric Scaled RoPE for cross-attention, which introduces a positional structure to facilitate sequential lyric-audio alignment learning. Furthermore, the model supports partial re-generation via span masking, enabling lyric-level editing while preserving the surrounding vocal style. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed model achieves high lyric fidelity, natural rap flow that is rhythmically coherent with the beat, and robust tempo control across a wide range of rapping styles and speeds.
entries.comment: Published in ISMIR 2026 (Best Paper Award nominee). Demo: https://bars-ismir2026.github.io/bars/
entries.journalRef: Proceedings of the 27th International Society for Music Information Retrieval Conference (ISMIR), 2026

entries.title: A Black-Box Reduction from Regret to Multi-Level Coverage
entries.abstract: Online Conformal Prediction (OCP) sequentially constructs prediction sets whose average empirical coverage converges to a target level over time, for arbitrary, potentially adversarial datasets. In the multi-level setting, prediction sets are produced at d coverage levels at once. Prior work argued for the use of online gradient descent with isotonic projections, which produces sets nested across levels, but with a √d dependence in the per-level coverage convergence rate. Here, we both generalize and improve prior work. First, we show that isotonic projections can be used for the construction of multi-level online conformal prediction sets from any online learning algorithm (not just gradient descent). Then, through a black-box reduction, we show that the linearized regret of the online algorithm itself automatically gives control over both per-level coverage and distributional consistency of multi-level predictions via Fenchel duality. Finally, by using the Weighted Interval Score, a standard scoring rule for assessing multi-level interval forecasts, we prove that these projections reduce both the size of the sets and their under-coverage. We study two instantiations of our theory, p-norm Online Mirror Descent and coordinate-wise Universal Portfolio methods, both improving the dependence on the number of levels to √logd for the multi-level OCP problem. Experiments on several datasets show favorable performance compared to baselines.

entries.title: Exact Natarajan Dimension of Homogeneous Multiclass Linear Predictors
entries.abstract: The Natarajan dimension is a fundamental measure of the capacity of multiclass hypothesis classes and plays an important role in analyzing their generalization ability. In this paper, by establishing lower and upper bounds, we show that the exact Natarajan dimension of homogeneous multiclass linear predictors with pairwise distinct class weights is n(k-1)-1, where n is the dimension of the feature space and k is the number of classes, for n,k≥3, n,k∈N.

entries.title: Low-rank Low Precision Training of Gaussian Processes
entries.abstract: Training Gaussian processes (GPs) at large scale is computationally challenging because evaluating the log-marginal likelihood and its gradients involves large, dense kernel matrices. We develop a scalable low-rank GP training approach that combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a fully independent training conditional (FITC) correction. The resulting objective and its analytic gradients can be evaluated using low-rank factors, diagonal quantities, and small dense matrices, without forming the full kernel matrix or its derivatives. The complete training procedure is implemented in single precision and evaluated on nine large-scale regression datasets. Across these problems, the method reaches the reference predictive accuracy while substantially reducing training time, although the required approximation rank varies across datasets. We also study the numerical behavior of the full-kernel predictive solve and show that single precision can become limiting for ill-conditioned problems. Finally, we investigate further reducing selected matrix operations to fp16 or TF32. These lower-precision variants provide only modest additional speedups and can become unreliable when the reduced system is poorly conditioned.

entries.title: BECON: Belief-Conditioned Constrained Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning under Drifting Preferences and Budgets
entries.abstract: Constrained preference-conditioned MORL typically assumes full task observability, treating preferences and safety budgets as stationary task signals. In real-world deployment, however, these signals are often unreliable proxies: intent may drift, safety tolerances may shift with context, and exposed descriptors may be noisy, delayed, or incomplete. We therefore formulate constrained preference-conditioned MORL as a partially observed task-specification problem, where the agent must navigate a fundamental conflict between unreliable external signals and latent interaction dynamics. We propose BECON, a belief-conditioned framework for constrained MORL with drifting preferences and budgets, which infers latent task context from recent histories to estimate preferences and safety budgets. These estimates are fused with the exposed task signal via uncertainty-dependent gates, enabling the policy to defer to observations under high epistemic uncertainty while correcting them when history is informative. The fused context jointly conditions preference optimization and context-adaptive constraint enforcement. Experiments on diverse multi-objective control tasks demonstrate that BECON consistently improves over state-of-the-art MORL baselines, achieving stronger robustness and constraint satisfaction under task drift.

entries.title: Scale-Invariant Empirical-Bayes Laplace Approximation for ReLU Networks
entries.abstract: ReLU networks are well-known to have continuous scale symmetries; infinitely many reparameterized weight vectors that represent the same function. Dinh et al. (2017) have shown that, by reparameterizing, the geometry of the loss landscape (e.g., curvature) of these networks can be changed arbitrarily without affecting the underlying function. Thus, any quantity that depends on the network's geometry should be defined with care. In this paper, we show that the Empirical Bayes (EB) Laplace's approximation is not well-defined for ReLU networks, mainly due to Hessian dependence in computing the marginal likelihood, which is not invariant under ReLU scale symmetries. Thus, we can get different prior precisions, posterior covariances, and predictive uncertainties for a network having identical predictions under ReLU scaling. We define family of prior precision fields indexed by γ and introduce γ-canonicalization, which first converts the network to its canonical representation by balancing the ratio of incoming to outgoing weights, and then fits the Empirical Bayes (EB) Laplace to the canonical representation. This procedure is equivalent to transporting the isotropic Gaussian prior from the canonical representation to the original coordinates, by producing a ReLU-scale-compatible precision field. This makes the marginal likelihood invariant under ReLU scaling, while allowing γ to be selected by maximizing the marginal likelihood. The resulting EB Laplace approximation is well-defined on ReLU scale-equivalence classes and yields consistent prior precision selection and predictive uncertainties across functionally identical parameterizations.

entries.title: MambaPD: Bidirectional Selective State Space Model for Parkinson's Disease Detection from Resting-State EEG
entries.abstract: Typical diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) occurs only after significant dopaminergic loss, while resting-state EEG abnormalities like alpha slowing and reduced coherence occur earlier. While many published EEG-based PD detectors claim accuracy greater than 95%, many use epoch-level splits which leak subject identity. I introduce MambaPD, a bidirectional selective state space model for resting-state EEG-based PD detection, blending the channel mixing, patch tokenization and bidirectional Mamba encoder. It is compared with four baselines (TCN, BiLSTM with attention, EEGNet and a patch Transformer) in two public datasets (UNM, SanDiego) using subject-independent 5-fold cross-validation (checkpoints were selected on the held-out fold, so absolute estimates are optimistic). On UNM the accuracy is between 0.67 and 0.71, and MambaPD (0.714) is not statistically distinguishable from the Transformer (0.715), and TCN (0.708), with the highest sensitivity (0.82), while the lowest specificity (0.52). For the smaller SanDiego cohort, accuracy is in the range of 0.60 to 0.70, with the highest scores (0.703) from TCN and the lowest (0.601) from EEGNet, while MambaPD scores 0.631, with the lowest specificity (0.46) among the five models. The differences among the models on UNM are minor compared to the differences among folds. I report the whole pipeline, per-fold results, and the shortcomings of the protocol.

entries.title: FocusBranch: Combinatorial Branch-and-Bound for ℓ₀ Neural Network Robustness Verification
entries.abstract: Verifying the local robustness of neural networks under ℓ₀ perturbations is inherently combinatorial, as it must reason over all sparse subsets of ε perturbed pixels. This paper presents FocusBranch, a combinatorial branch-and-bound framework for ℓ₀ robustness verification. The key insight is to make the ℓ₀-ball decomposable and branchable using a node abstraction, which consists of a focus pixel set S and a level l, permitting at most ε-l pixels outside S. This abstraction unifies two branching mechanisms: concrete nodes branch through upper shadows to fix additional perturbed locations, while super nodes branch through covering designs to cover many perturbation cases with fewer child nodes. FocusBranch proves node safety by concretizing linear relaxations over node-constrained ℓ₀-balls and recursively branches on unknown nodes. Rather than relying on a fixed verification plan, it samples nodes across levels to estimate safe rates and costs, then selects a starting level and branching strategy predicted to minimize verification time. Experiments on fully connected and convolutional classifiers for MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 show that FocusBranch verifies ℓ₀ robustness effectively across architectures and outperforms state-of-the-art verifiers. The code is available at: https://github.com/simpl-group/FocusBranch.
entries.comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 32 pages, 11 figures, 6 tables

entries.title: Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization
entries.abstract: Many real-world applications require language models to internalize knowledge that was absent from pretraining, to incorporate continually updated facts, or to learn new domain skills. Self-distillation has emerged as a natural approach for this task. A model conditioned on the source material acts as the teacher, and an unconditioned student is trained to reproduce the teacher's behavior closed-book. We propose Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD), an efficient per-token mixed-policy method for self-distillation. The student generates each rollout by default, while the teacher intervenes only at positions where its next-token distribution substantially diverges from the student's. Unlike off-policy distillation with teacher-generated prefixes, this design keeps training rollouts close to the student's test-time behavior, while avoiding the low-signal states that fully on-policy rollouts drift into. In effect, SSD lets the teacher steer the rollout exactly where the privileged context changes the prediction. On three closed-book QA benchmarks measuring fact recall, knowledge updates, and skill acquisition, SSD nearly matches on-policy distillation while using 38-69% fewer supervised tokens and consistently outperforms off-policy distillation on the held-out test set. On a forgetting stress test, SSD retains the most general capability while also achieving the best in-domain accuracy and using less supervision than the on-policy baseline. Overall, SSD establishes a new accuracy-efficiency-forgetting Pareto frontier for self-distillation.
entries.comment: NeurIPS 2026. 26 pages, 8 figures, 12 tables. Project page: https://ssd-distill.github.io/ Code: https://github.com/ShayanTalaei/SpeculativeSelfDistillation

entries.title: Benchmarking language models and agents for scientific reasoning in evolving materials laboratories
entries.abstract: Large language models and the multi-agent systems built around them could accelerate materials discovery by connecting scientific knowledge with experimental decisions. Existing benchmarks establish capabilities in domain knowledge, multimodal interpretation and scientific tool use. As language models increasingly support materials research workflows, their ability to distinguish closely related material states and reason accurately with quantitative evidence remains insufficiently evaluated. These abilities are essential for comparing material responses, assessing mechanisms and maintaining reliable judgements as experimental evidence accumulates. We introduce MatScope to evaluate three connected capabilities. M1 tests unaided, condition-specific reasoning through 200 tasks spanning ten research functions, using aluminium and high-entropy alloys as representative material systems. M2 tests agent-assisted transfer of related knowledge to unresolved materials questions. MatEvoBench-20 tests initial forecasts across scientific dependency chains and revisions of still-hidden responses as observations accumulate. Across eleven model deployments, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, given-input calculations and many physical explanations are handled well. Fine-grained response estimates, comparisons between similar states and quantitatively supported choices remain substantially weaker. Related literature improves selected estimates, while condition and baseline mismatches limit transfer. Progressive observations calibrate some downstream responses and destabilize earlier accurate predictions. MatScope establishes measurable targets for developing reliable scientific reasoning in future self-evolving materials laboratories and materials-aware world models.

entries.title: Scalable Bayesian Optimization for Efficient Exploration of Moire Patterns
entries.abstract: Large materials design spaces often contain rare high-performing configurations that are difficult to identify through trial-and-error exploration or purely representative machine-learning (ML) sampling. In this work, we present FruBO, a flexible Bayesian Optimization framework for accelerating the discovery of optimal configurations in computationally demanding materials design problems. As a case study, we investigate multilayer Moiré patterns generated by the superposition of six rotated hexagonal lattices, where the objective is to identify the rotational conformation that maximizes pore-size uniformity, quantified using the Jain fairness index. The resulting benchmark contains 600,000 unique configurations and exhibits a highly skewed objective distribution, making the global optimum difficult to locate by random sampling. We compare random exploration, Gaussian Process-based Bayesian Optimization, and Bayesian Optimization using a lightweight CatBoost surrogate with committee-based uncertainty estimation. Random sampling identifies the global optimum only after 533,012 evaluations, requiring approximately 31 hours, while Gaussian Process-based BO becomes impractical due to GPU memory exhaustion after 290 acquired samples. In contrast, FruBO with CatBoost identifies the global optimum after 1,470 acquired samples and approximately 1.15 hours. These results demonstrate that scalable surrogate models can substantially improve the feasibility and efficiency of BO in large nanomaterials design spaces.

entries.title: HyPLM Technical Report
entries.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are standard tools for variant-effect prediction, protein annotation and design, but the compute needed to train and serve them keeps growing. We present HyPLM-Flash, an efficient and open PLM trained by Hyra 2.0, the research agent developed by our team. HyPLM-Flash is a 650-million-parameter masked language model trained on 726 billion tokens, 0.73 times the data of ESM-2 650M and a fifth to an eighth of the data of E1-600M and ESM C 600M. It runs on an inference engine with fused kernels and INT8 matrix multiplication, embedding about 130,000 residues per second on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU, 1.9 to 2.7 times faster than other 600M-class encoders. In a matched evaluation against 28 public checkpoints on 32 tasks, HyPLM-Flash reaches a ProteinGym zero-shot Spearman correlation of 0.409, statistically tied with ESM-2 650M, ESM C 600M and E1-600M, and the highest organismal-fitness score among self-supervised single-sequence models. It gives the best long-range contact precision of all models evaluated, including ESM-2 15B and ESM C 6B, and a lower masked-residue loss than ESM-2 650M, ESM C 600M and E1-600M on held-out sequences and on recently released PDB chains. Matching state-of-the-art accuracy at a fraction of the training and inference cost, HyPLM-Flash sets a new Pareto frontier for protein language models. We have released the model weights and the inference engine at https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/hyra-results/tree/main.

entries.title: Reward-Estimated Hypergradient for Bilevel Reinforcement Learning with Black-Box Follower
entries.abstract: Hypergradient (HG) methods for bilevel reinforcement learning (RL) typically assume a white-box follower whose reward is known. In practice, however, the leader rarely knows the follower's reward function and can only observe its trajectories. We address this black-box setting and propose Reward-Estimated Hypergradients (RE-HG), which recovers the follower's reward from these trajectories via inverse RL (IRL). Yet IRL identifies the reward only up to potential-based shaping, a transformation that leaves the follower's behavior unchanged but biases the HG. We prove that, for linear rewards, this bias cancels when IRL estimates are aggregated across sufficiently diverse dynamics, which the leader's own updates naturally supply. To handle finite samples, RE-HG truncates small eigenvalues of the aggregated feature covariance, restoring the identifiable subspace and stabilizing the estimation. Experiments show that RE-HG estimates gradients aligned with a white-box Oracle and achieves comparable performance; empirically, the truncation also suppresses HG explosions, letting RE-HG avoid local optima that trap the Oracle in sharp reward landscapes.

entries.title: HyInv Technical Report
entries.abstract: Inverse folding designs amino-acid sequences for a given protein backbone, and screening needs many candidates that are both diverse and well folded. We present HyInv, a 1.96-million-parameter backbone-conditioned graph network with an encoder-decoder architecture, trained by Hyra 2.0, the research agent developed by our team: pretrained with random-order autoregressive sequence modeling, followed by structure-reward reinforcement learning. At inference, a grouped draft-and-rewrite sampler that uses separate draft and rewrite temperatures improves refolding TM-score at matched diversity. An optimized implementation with BF16 numerics designs 128 sequences for a 402-residue backbone in 50.6 ms on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU, about 52 times faster than the reference sampler, and an exact FP32 path that returns the reference sequences is 8.7 times faster. Across five benchmark datasets and seven dataset-predictor combinations, HyInv reaches a higher average scTM than all ten external baselines at comparable or higher sequence diversity, with large margins over ProteinMPNN and ProteinZero V2. The same default setting supports de novo backbones, pocket-constrained libraries, enzyme redesign with the catalytic site kept, and loop redesign. We have released our code and model at https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hyra-results/tree/main/AI4Science/hyinv.

entries.title: MUTE: Multi-Level Alignment Uncoupling Against Talking-Head Exploitation for Voice Protection
entries.abstract: Talking-head generation models, which synthesize realistic facial animations from audio, are increasingly vulnerable to misuse in multimodal deepfake scenarios. Protecting such systems remains challenging, as talking-head models fundamentally rely on precise audio-visual alignment, while effective audio protection methods remain largely underexplored. In this work, we propose MUTE, an audio protection framework that uncouples the underlying audio-visual alignment through a multi-level strategy. Specifically, MUTE combines (1) Alignment-level Disruption, which directly perturbs cross-modal attention to disrupt structural alignment, and (2) Representation-level Degradation, which perturbs temporal audio embeddings to degrade their representations. To improve robustness, perturbations are constrained in the STFT domain to high-energy regions, making them resistant to post-processing, denoising, and adaptive attacks. An optional speaker-level objective further mitigates potential bypass via TTS-based resynthesis. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MUTE consistently degrades lip synchronization across both white-box and black-box talking-head models while preserving perceptual audio quality. The proposed method remains effective under real-world transformations and can be combined with image-based approaches to provide stronger multimodal protection. The source code and project page are available at https://github.com/jindl465/MUTE.
entries.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 33 pages, including appendix and checklist. Project and code: https://github.com/jindl465/MUTE

entries.title: Trajectory Density Ratios under Weak Support: A Survey across the Sciences
entries.abstract: Many problems across the sciences compare two stochastic processes through the sequences they generate. Reinforcement learning asks what a new policy would return from the trajectories of an old one; molecular simulation asks how much more a ligand binds from samples of the unbound state; climate attribution asks how a heat wave shifted under warming; and language-model post-training asks what a deployed agent will do from logged interactions. In every case, one quantity would answer all these questions at once: the ratio of the two probability laws over their generated sequences, the trajectory density ratio. This ratio exists only under strong conditions. When one process reaches states the other cannot, the ratio does not exist; when their overlap is thin, its variance grows without control with the sequence length; and when they concentrate on different lower-dimensional sets, the ratio is undefined altogether. Weak support of this kind is the norm for sequence data, not a sampling accident, and its price is paid in identifiability rather than in noise alone. This survey organizes the field around a three-level diagnosis of weak support and a map of the nine retreats that methods take when the full ratio is out of reach, from direct estimation and reweighting through staged decomposition, stationarization, and partial-identification bounds to smoothing, transport couplings, operator spectra, and direct estimation of a single functional. Each retreat keeps part of what the ratio offers and pays for the rest, and each application domain has standardized the retreat its data force. The survey closes with open problems: testable diagnostics at every level, partial identification at the trajectory level, a rate theory of time-amplified error, and benchmarks with ground truth.

entries.title: FireGate: Bounding Behaviour Change Before Training in Continual RL Fine-Tuning
entries.abstract: Fine-tuning a deployed language model on one task after another can change behaviour that should stay fixed, such as earlier skills, general chat or refusals. Today, such forgetting is found only after training, on the benchmarks someone chose to run. This work bounds, before training, how often its outputs change on chosen prompt distributions. FireGate places each task's update, such as a new LoRA, behind a gate, which is a classifier on the model's frozen lower layers that decides for each prompt whether the update is used. Where no gate fires, the model computes exactly what the old one computes. As a result, on any prompt distribution, every bounded behaviour score changes by at most the gates' firing rate there over a whole task stream. Calibrating each gate on unlabeled prompts of what must not change fixes that rate before training, with a PAC guarantee, whatever weights training produces. Forgetting is thus bounded by the gate's false-alarm rate, and its price is the gate's power: no update, gated or not, that changes as few protected outputs can change new-task outputs more often than the best test of that level tells new-task prompts from protected ones. On reinforcement-learning streams of up to five tasks, gated training keeps the earlier tasks and changes 3.3% of held-out chat responses, whereas ungated training changes 91.8%. Across seven models, the gain kept behind the gate follows its firing rate on new-task prompts, measured before training. The certificate covers the gated model as deployed, on the prompt distributions sampled for calibration, not against an adversary who searches for prompts that fire the gate.

entries.title: MixRoute: Rethinking Single-Distribution Training for Generalizable Neural Routing
entries.abstract: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) is a promising paradigm for solving routing problems, yet its generalization across diverse data distributions remains a critical bottleneck. Existing methods typically tackle cross-distribution generalization through complex multi-distribution training or intricate meta-learning schemes, implicitly presuming that single-distribution training yields a weak zero-shot baseline. In this paper, we demonstrate that the potential of single-distribution training has been substantially underestimated and can be unlocked by a simple architectural inductive bias: Mix Normalization. To approach this, we first construct a comprehensive benchmark spanning three representative routing problems and 179 fine-grained datasets, capturing diverse shifts in node coordinates, customer demands, capacity and time windows. Building on this benchmark, we propose MixRoute, a neural framework that adaptively combines normalization statistics at different granularities to mitigate varying distribution shifts. Trained exclusively on uniform distributions, MixRoute generalizes effectively to a wide range of unseen distributions without any distribution-specific adaptation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MixRoute consistently achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot generalization. Our work revisits normalization as a parsimonious alternative for zero-shot generalization against complex training-adaptation schemes.

entries.title: ShiftCache: Fast and Exact Indel Effect Prediction by Reusing Shifted Reference Encodings
entries.abstract: Sequence-to-function models such as AlphaGenome and Borzoi read up to a megabase of DNA and score a genetic variant by comparing their predictions for the reference and alternate sequences. Insertions and deletions (indels) are costly to score, because an indel usually shifts the unchanged DNA after it onto a different pooling grid, which prevents direct reuse of the reference's encoder activations. The AlphaGenome Atlas scored more than 100 million indels with three full model passes each, although the DNA after an indel matches the reference shifted by the indel's length. We present ShiftCache, an exact reuse system that encodes each shifted reference once and shares it among all variants scored in the same window with the same shift. ShiftCache copies every encoder output a variant can reuse and recomputes the rest in batched tiles. On held-out AlphaGenome windows shared by many indels, in strict fp32 on one A6000, ShiftCache is 3.5 to 6.5× faster than deduplicated dense execution and 1.6 to 2.7× faster than our adaptation of layer-by-layer reuse to indels. It is 3.5 to 4.1× faster than dense reimplementations of two published analyses with Borzoi and AlphaGenome, and 2.6× faster than dense execution with Enformer. Scoring each variant in its own centered 131 kb window makes ShiftCache only 1.36× faster than deduplicated dense execution, and highly diverse insertion lengths or many dispersed edits can make it slower than layer-by-layer reuse or dense execution. For encoders that meet our conditions, ShiftCache computes the same predictions as dense execution in exact arithmetic.
