We further demonstrate the dataset's unique utility with two complementary applications: deriving semantic directions in the latent space for brain-supervised image editing, and conditioning a generative model on brain-decoded labels for brain-supervised image generation. Our dataset paves the way for advancing brain-computer interfaces (BCI) for semantic-level visual saliency detection and brain-supervised generative modeling. Our dataset and code are openly released at OSF (https://osf.io/2guk3/) and at HuggingFace https://huggingface.co/datasets/yefllower/EEGFaceSem.
entries.comment: 18 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Evaluations and Datasets Track. Conference page: https://neurips.cc/virtual/2026/loc/paris/poster/138993 ; Project page: https://EEGFaceSem.github.io/

entries.title: Universal Approximation by Equivariant Message-Passing Graph Neural Networks with a Bilinear Readout
entries.abstract: We prove universal approximation for the bilinear-readout equivariant message-passing network (BREMP), a reference architecture for equivariant graph neural network interatomic potentials. Its layers combine equivariant convolutions with affine maps, and its readout forms invariants from products of the equivariant features. We construct a one-layer feature that determines the local environment up to permutations of atoms of the same type. The construction uses spherical harmonic filters of degree no larger than the largest number of neighbors at a common distance from the center. Iterating the construction recovers the environment reachable in as many hops as there are layers, using the same bound on filter degrees at the layer cutoff. The readout approximates every continuous invariant function of the features uniformly on compact sets. Together these give universal approximation of atomic energies at a prescribed physical range using a shorter layer cutoff. We assume that, throughout the admissible class, message passing reaches all neighbors in each physical environment within a common number of layers. Finally, DPA4, an interatomic potential architecture in production use, inherits this result by approximating the BREMP layers constructed in the proof and realizing the bilinear readout.

entries.title: How reliable is an embedding of the seabed? Repeat-look measurement of frozen encoders on synthetic aperture sonar
entries.abstract: Pretrained encoders from self-supervised representation learning are increasingly applied to sonar imagery of the seafloor, where they are evaluated with protocols that take one embedding per target. A target patch of seabed, by contrast, is re-imaged from an alternate look on overlapping survey passes, so each embedding is one measurement of that target. Standard protocols cannot say how consistent those measurements are, or how much of their spread belongs to the patch and how much to the acquisition geometry. We treat this as a measurement-reliability problem. Using a synthetic-aperture sonar (SAS) survey, we measure the repeat-look reliability of embeddings from a frozen natural-image encoder (DINOv3 ViT-S/16). Standard single-look metrics, effective rank, clustering and a linear probe for coral, are all stable to the look, and the probe performs well (AUC 0.93). Yet the repeat-look reliability of the same embeddings is poor, with a distance-based intraclass correlation (dbICC) of 0.20 and nearest neighbours and clusters that barely agree across looks. This contradiction resolves as we find the probe learns a stable direction, whose ICC of 0.60 is 3.0 times that of the full embedding. Variance components, calculated from generalizability theory, attribute under a tenth of the within-cell spread to look acquisition geometry. The rest is cell-specific and cannot be separated without repeat passes at matched geometry. A sonar-pretrained encoder (BenthicDINO) and a classical SAS texture descriptor show the same pattern. For this dataset and the tested representations, uses that depend on patch identity fail, such as cross-pass comparison and retrieval, while uses at the level of habitat type (e.g. coral classification) do not. Because the standard metrics did not detect this, we argue that repeat-look reliability should accompany any evaluation of representations of the seafloor.
entries.comment: Accepted at the Maritime Computer Vision Workshop (MaCVi) at WACV 2027

entries.title: BAPLe++: Cross-Model Transferability and Prompt-Level Defense of Backdoors in Medical Foundation Models
entries.abstract: Medical foundation models (Med-FMs) are increasingly adapted to clinical tasks through prompt learning, which tunes a small set of prompt tokens while the backbone remains frozen. Recent work has shown that this efficiency introduces a vulnerability: jointly optimizing learnable prompts and an imperceptible noise trigger during few-shot adaptation implants a backdoor that leaves clean performance intact but steers triggered inputs to an attacker-chosen class. Since prompts are compact and readily shared, this raises two questions: whether a backdoored prompt remains effective on a different Med-FM, and whether it can be repaired without retraining the backbone. We address both in BAPLe++. First, we present the first study of cross-model transferability of prompt-based backdoors, quantified by two proposed metrics, Clean Accuracy Difference (CAD) and Backdoor Accuracy Difference (BAD). Second, we propose DePLe (Defense via Prompt Learning), which uses the infected prompt as a fixed anchor and learns a new prompt on a small clean set that preserves the clean task while diverging from the compromised embedding region. Experiments on four Med-FMs and six chest X-ray and histopathology datasets show that backdoors transfer across models, but asymmetrically and in a dataset-dependent manner. Compared with four training-free input transformations, DePLe reduces backdoor accuracy more consistently while preserving, and in several settings improving, clean accuracy. Our code can be accessed on https://github.com/Ufaqkhan/Baple-Plus-Plus

entries.title: ConwayNet: Interpretability, Activation Coherence, and Noise Resilience via a Game-of-Life-Inspired Lateral Inhibition in Artificial Neural Networks
entries.abstract: Deep neural networks achieve universal function approximation by stacking interconnected nonlinearities, but as a consequence they are sensitive to noise and resist mechanistic interpretation. In contrast, the local update rules of cellular automata, such as Conway's Game of Life, give rise to not merely interpretable but programmable dynamics. We explore a bridge between these worlds: a lateral inhibition in neural networks based on continuous Game-of-Life rules that derives inhibitory and excitatory responses from the layer input and blends them into the activation map in a state-conditioned way. The mechanism is differentiable and architecture-agnostic, and its regulation is imposed rather than learned: the rule's parameters are fixed and are not optimised, while the rule's values and derivatives shape training throughout the network. Wired into fully connected, convolutional, wide-residual and graph convolutional networks, it gives rise to several properties. Activation maps become coherent across space, depth and seeds, with coarse structure persisting through depth while fine detail is renewed at every layer. The co-activation graph of the hidden units departs from an Erdős–Rényi random graph: it is laid out on the image and its giant component grows in steps, as in a spatial graph. Networks started from nearly identical initialisations, under label noise, disagree on thirty times fewer test images. Saliency maps rest on the object rather than the background, and resilience to pixel noise not seen in training is substantially improved.

entries.title: Constrained Look-ahead Guidance for Interference-Aware Flow Editing
entries.abstract: Diffusion and flow models enable powerful generative modeling, but controlled editing remains challenging due to the need to balance source fidelity and edit compliance along the generative trajectory. We propose a principled, inversion-free framework for flow-based image editing from a trajectory centric perspective. Rather than relying on inversion or heuristic guidance, we introduce a one-step look-ahead mechanism that evaluates the effect of candidate updates on both edit and fidelity rewards estimated via denoising, and adjusts the current update based on this evaluation. At each step, our method applies reward-driven corrections guided by the look-ahead evaluation under an explicit fidelity constraint, resulting in stable and coherent trajectory evolution. This look-ahead design mitigates gradient interference between edit and fidelity objectives by anticipating their interaction in future states, leading to improved trade-offs. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves stronger semantic edits while better preserving source content compared to existing strong baselines.

entries.title: AERO: Adaptive Ensemble-Disagreement Routing for Oracle Feedback in Sample-Efficient Online RLHF
entries.abstract: Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has driven substantial improvements across a wide range of tasks, but the cost of acquiring preference labels remains the dominant bottleneck in the alignment pipeline. While many recent alignment methods improve sample efficiency through active exploration over candidate responses, they typically query the oracle uniformly across contexts, even for contexts where the learned reward estimates are already reliable enough to provide synthetic labels. We propose Adaptive Ensemble-disagreement Routing for Oracle feedback (AERO), a fully online RLHF algorithm built on a Dyna-style model-based RL architecture, in which an ensemble-based Epistemic Reward Model (ERM) serves both as a reward posterior for exploration and as a learned preference-feedback model for synthetic labeling. AERO uses ensemble vote entropy, a Query-by-Committee disagreement measure, combined with an adaptive thresholding mechanism to decide which contexts require oracle feedback and which can instead receive ERM-based synthetic preference labels, concentrating expensive labels where they are most informative. Empirical results across different model families and scales show that AERO achieves highly competitive alignment performance while reducing the required oracle-query budget compared to online DPO and strong active-exploration baselines.

entries.title: Writer-independent handedness identification from offline Bangla handwriting under controlled acquisition
entries.abstract: Handedness is a soft-biometric cue for forensic document examination and writer profiling, yet reported accuracies from offline handwriting rarely keep writers, texts and image acquisition apart, so models may recognise the writer or capture conditions rather than the writing hand. Such controlled evidence is missing for Bangla. Using our BanglaHand dataset of 42 writers (21 left- and 21 right-handed), who each wrote six shared prompts and two own texts under controlled collection and photography, we evaluate handedness identification with all images of each test writer held out, whole-writer permutation tests and photometric controls. An ink-gradient descriptor identified the handedness of unseen writers with 77.4% balanced accuracy (95% writer-bootstrap interval 67.7-86.5%; p=0.001) and frozen ImageNet embeddings with 69.5-72.0%. Part of this signal is stroke darkness: in a post hoc analysis, right-handed writers' strokes were darker at their centres for equal stroke width, consistent with higher pen pressure and not explained by lighting drift. With ink density and brightness regressed out, the descriptor still reached 64.5% (p=0.027), whereas writing-only shape features were weaker (60.8%; p=0.090). Handedness is thus identifiable from offline Bangla handwriting under controlled acquisition, and photometric controls are essential to interpret such cues.

entries.title: Matchability-Aware Conformal Prediction for Open-Ended Language Model Generation
entries.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often do not produce calibrated uncertainty estimates for their answers. We propose CAELUM, a framework that builds semantic prediction sets while separating aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty. CAELUM samples answers using an ensemble of clarification prompts, clusters them by semantic equivalence, and estimates the aleatoric and epistemic components via kernel-based von Neumann entropy before calibrating nonconformity scores with split conformal prediction. We use a weight w_λ(x)=1+U_ale(x)+λ U_epi(x) to control for the contribution of the epistemic uncertainty of each instance and fit a coefficient λ* to minimize prediction set size. When the objective is nonflat and selection is stable across splits, λ* could be a diagnostic, where large values may indicate epistemic dominance (retrieve, abstain) and λ*→0 aleatoric dominance (clarify). For individual queries, a log ratio R(x) compares the weighted epistemic component with the aleatoric component. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the coverage is capped by matchability, the fraction of items whose reference answer appears in any sampled cluster. Empirically, this matchability can be predicted from the original question features using a lightweight classifier. We use those predictions to define a stratum and derive a conformal coverage bound within it. Across 30 LLM and dataset combinations (4-32B), mean coverage is 0.74 in the learned stratum versus 0.65 overall, averaged over the 78 evaluations using the learned classifier. Project page: https://unco3892.github.io/caelum/
entries.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://unco3892.github.io/caelum/

entries.title: Spectrogram-Based CNN Autoencoder for One-Class Anomaly Detection in Machining Vibration Signals
entries.abstract: This work presents a one-class anomaly detection framework for vibration-based condition monitoring in machining processes using a convolutional neural network autoencoder. Three-axis vibration signals acquired during industrial broaching are transformed into time–frequency spectrograms and combined into a compact three-channel representation, enabling convolutional feature learning on multivariate time-series data. The autoencoder is trained exclusively on normal process data and detects anomalous strokes based on reconstruction errors. Labeled validation data are used for threshold calibration and an independent test set is reserved for final performance evaluation. To improve sensitivity to short-lived process instabilities such as chatter, a localized residual-based metric termed Segmented Vertical Error (SVE) is introduced. Experimental results on approximately 10,000 broaching strokes show a clear separation between normal and anomalous process conditions under strong class imbalance. The processing pipeline is additionally evaluated on an external public turning dataset as a proof of concept, indicating preliminary applicability beyond the original broaching setup. The results suggest that spectrogram-based autoencoder models can provide a practical and scalable basis for one-class anomaly detection in industrial vibration monitoring.

entries.title: Breaking Precision Walls in First-, Second-, and Zeroth-Order Optimizers: One Constant, Set in Advance
entries.abstract: Under power-law signal decay across directions, an optimizer can fit strong directions and miss weak ones while average loss hides it. A precision wall measures the steepest decay where the weakest direction recovers within 5% in a fixed budget. On low-rank matrix sensing and quadratics one constant sets the wall: once it dominates the denominator, Adam or grafted Shampoo is momentum descent at step η/c, setting the wall; in Shampoo, matching grafting's constant to damping restores the wall after three hypotheses failed. In zeroth-order Adam, ε acts against ε from a mean-square spectral model; below ε error hits a noise floor. Set from true curvature or spectrum on new shapes, the rule raised the wall above the same-step default by a forecast amount: on two sensing shapes by 1.96, 1.15 (Adam) and 1.59, 1.74 (grafted Shampoo), and on two Hadamard-rotated quadratics by 1.12, 0.73 (zeroth-order Adam, longer budget), rising on all seeds; fixed-step momentum at that step reaches those walls. A cosine-scheduled default (small constant giving weak modes large steps) is higher on one sensing shape, matched on new seeds of the other, and lower with the rule's constant. A default step retuned per budget catches up on rotated quadratics and population logistic regression, fails at 1 query/step on two diagonal quadratics (catching up at 16), and exceeds the rule on digits logistic regression (full-batch and minibatches, where gradient noise sets the η= 0.01, 0.1 default walls). On logistic regression the rule did not raise the first-order wall: same-step default Adam was higher (its wall on 4 new shapes at the forecast stability limit), while in zeroth order on the population loss setting ε raised the wall by 0.98, 0.88.

entries.title: CyberBinGym: Can AI Agents Turn Binary Patches into Real Exploits?
entries.abstract: Security fixes usually reach users as compiled updates, but deployment delays leave unpatched systems exposed. During this window, comparing patched and unpatched binaries can reveal how to exploit a vulnerability, turning a defensive update into actionable information for attackers. Existing benchmarks do not measure this capability: they expose source code, rely on human-crafted challenges, or evaluate binary comprehension without requiring exploitation. We introduce CyberBinGym, a benchmark containing 100 tasks derived from real vulnerabilities in 53 widely used projects, spanning six vulnerability families and three levels of analysis complexity. Agents receive stripped vulnerable and patched binaries without source code or vulnerability information, and must combine static and dynamic analysis to recover and exploit the vulnerability. Evaluation separately measures vulnerability recovery through differential crash testing and end-to-end exploitation through flag retrieval, with trajectory audits to reject reward hacking. The strongest evaluated agent recovers the target vulnerability in 88% of tasks and exploits it in 20%. Providing the patched binary raises its exploit rate from 10% to 25% on a matched 20-task subset; with standard binary hardening enabled, it still exploits two of its 20 previously successful tasks. These results demonstrate that current agents can turn released binary patches into working exploits in a controlled setting, although exploitation remains unreliable. These capabilities lower the barriers to targeting unpatched software and compress defenders' effective response window, increasing the urgency of timely patch deployment.

entries.title: FedSGN: Federated Sparse Grassmann Newton Learning for IoT Anomaly Detection
entries.abstract: Anomaly detection plays a critical role in securing the Internet of things (IoT). Although existing federated principal component analysis (PCA) methods can learn the subspace of normal samples without sharing raw data, they often suffer from feature redundancy that may degrade detection performance. To address this limitation, we propose a novel and effective federated sparse Grassmann Newton (FedSGN) learning method for IoT anomaly detection. Technically, our FedSGN leverages the ℓ_(2,0)-norm constraint on the global projection matrix to eliminate redundancy and introduces an orthogonality penalty to preserve the intrinsic structure. Moreover, we develop an augmented Lagrangian solver integrated with a semismooth Newton scheme to enable parallel client updates and Grassmann projection for robustness. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves favorable overall detection performance while reducing communication overhead. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/xianchaoxiu/FedSGN

entries.title: AbductionBench: Benchmarking Abductive Reasoning in Large Language Models
entries.abstract: Abductive reasoning is the inference of plausible explanations for observed evidence. Evaluating this capability requires more than a single task: a system may need to generate an explanation, discriminate among competing hypotheses, revise its hypotheses as evidence arrives, or decide what evidence to seek next. Yet these capabilities are typically evaluated through isolated benchmarks with different task formulations and scoring procedures, so claims that a model is “good at abduction” may reflect only a narrow aspect of this capability. We introduce AbductionBench, a unified framework whose taxonomy characterizes abductive tasks. We instantiate this framework on 27 datasets spanning ten domains and evaluate eight LLMs from four model families evaluated on single-choice selection tasks. Beyond harmonizing heterogeneous tasks, AbductionBench separates final-answer evaluation from analysis of the observable reasoning traces and interaction histories produced alongside those answers. We analyze written traces as observable model outputs rather than faithful representations of internal computation, characterizing evidence use, hypothesis comparison, uncertainty, contradiction handling, and answer commitment. Jev matches or exceeds small LLMs when selecting among explanations over compact evidence but falls substantially behind on longer cases, suggesting that candidate discrimination and extended evidence integration place different demands on a system. In interactive tasks, the proportion of actions judged relevant declines at later steps, and a relevant first question is associated with a correct final answer; in the passive task, models rarely revise their initial hypothesis as new evidence arrives. Together, these findings highlight the value of evaluating abductive reasoning through both final answers and observable evidence use, hypothesis revision, and information gathering.

entries.title: Spectral Bias Reduction in Local Gated ReLU Architectures
entries.abstract: Neural networks trained by gradient-based methods learn the low-frequency content of a target function faster than its high-frequency content. This spectral bias is well documented, but it is much less clear which architectural choices mitigate it and which cannot. We study the question for shallow ReLU models linear in their trainable parameters, where each mode is learned at a rate given by a Gram-matrix eigenvalue, and for a general symmetric bilinear form a(·,·), so that least-squares regression (a= the L² inner product) and variational or physics-informed losses (a= the H¹ energy form) are two instances of one analysis. Within this framework we propose gated local ReLU dictionaries, obtained by multiplying each ReLU feature by a hat partition-of-unity weight, in the spirit of partition-of-unity finite elements and overlapping Schwarz methods. The resulting Gram matrices are block-banded for any local bilinear form, with a block-Toeplitz interior whose matrix-valued symbol governs the spectrum. The two forms then behave very differently. For L² regression, the symbol is bounded away from zero, the ratio is uniform in the number of windows, and the measured spread of frequency-dependent learning rates falls from 1.9×10⁵ to 4.5 at matched model size. For the H¹ stiffness matrix, the symbol vanishes at zero frequency: gating leaves the Θ(N²) conditioning intact and inverts the frequency ordering instead of removing the bias. A preconditioner built from the same interior stencil will fix the spectral bias, showing that architecture alone is not enough. Experiments on 1D regression and Poisson problems confirm the dichotomy, and the regression effect persists when the hidden-layer parameters are trained as well.
entries.comment: 24 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Preliminary version; comments welcome

entries.title: A Geometric Theory for Nonequilibrium Transformer Dynamics
entries.abstract: We develop a variational and geometric theory based on statistical physics for the joint evolution of Transformer attention and token representations at fixed model parameters. To this end, we introduce a free energy for the attention and model the evolution of the attention weights by its Fisher–Rao gradient flow. At fixed token representations, we prove that the softmax matrix is the unique free-energy minimiser and that every positive attention trajectory converges to it. For prescribed time-dependent representations, we show that the attention dynamics becomes linear after a change to logit variables. This result yields tracking bounds relative to the instantaneous softmax and sufficient conditions for attention to converge to a fixed matrix. Hamiltonian dynamics for the representations and their momenta are then coupled to the attention relaxation driven by the same energy. This coupling results in an energy-dissipation law. We also develop two alternative Hamiltonians incorporating the attention value map. We prove global well-posedness of the attention flow and all three coupled systems.
entries.comment: 29 pages Submitted to Proc Roy Soc A

entries.title: Audit Before You Merge: Provenance, Probing, and Continual LoRA Composition
entries.abstract: Post-hoc merging of public LoRA adapters is an attractive gradient-free path to continual adaptation, but reliable measurement of catastrophic forgetting in this setting depends on infrastructure that prior work has not addressed. We treat each adapter merge as a sequential task in a continual-learning setting, with the instruction-tuned base model's capabilities as Task 0, and study forgetting on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Public adapter hubs contain modules that fail basic provenance checks: silent base-version mismatches and near-zero delta norms whose inclusion inflates measured interference by ~10pp. We propose a two-check audit (base-model match, non-trivial delta norm) and a leakage-free probing protocol as preconditions for any forgetting study in this setting. On an audited 4-adapter set, naive merging causes -10.5pp on GSM8K and -18.3pp on HumanEval, while Task Arithmetic at lambda=0.5 sits within a standard error of the unmerged baseline. A coordinate search including negative coefficients identifies the math adapter as probe-optimal at lambda=-0.5, outside the reach of positive-only mergers, suggesting forgetting has structure that negation-aware merging may exploit. The same protocol replicates on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, where 2 of 4 candidate adapters fail the audit and the audited merge reproduces the same merge-method ranking on GSM8K, supporting that our findings are not Llama-specific.
entries.comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 17 tables. ICML 2026 Workshop on Continual Adaptation at Scale (CATS). Code: https://github.com/LennyAharon/audit_continual_learning

entries.title: Safe Offline Reinforcement Learning using Behavior Regularisation and Latent Feasibility Guidance
entries.abstract: Safe offline reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to learn policies that maximize return while satisfying safety constraints, using a static dataset. To characterize state-wise safety, reachability analysis identifies the feasible region, defined as the set of states from which constraints can be satisfied at every future step. Policies are commonly extracted from learned value functions with advantage-weighted regression (AWR). However, AWR relies on exponentiated weights that amplify value estimation errors, whereas behavior-regularized policy gradient methods directly utilize the action gradient of the value function and often make more effective use of learned critics. We propose Feasibility-Optimized Conditional Actor Learning (FOCAL), a method that incorporates behavior-regularized policy gradients into a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) actor. FOCAL optimizes this policy using a first-order objective partitioned by feasibility, updating the actor to increase return on transitions estimated to be feasible and to reduce constraint violations on transitions estimated to be infeasible. During inference, FOCAL dynamically adjusts the scale of the latent prior according to the estimated feasibility of the state to adjust the conservatism of action sampling. Theoretically, we show that for AWR, the policy update variance depends exponentially on the advantage error, whereas for FOCAL it scales linearly with the variance of the value estimation error. Across the DSRL benchmark, FOCAL satisfies the constraints on all evaluated tasks while achieving competitive or higher returns compared to baselines.

entries.title: Causal Heteroscedastic Structure Learning From Incomplete Temporal data
entries.abstract: Discovering causal structures in multivariate time series (MTS) is critical in domains such as finance and neuroscience, yet remains challenging in practice due to three distinct obstacles. First, MTS are routinely corrupted by missing values, where naive impute-then-discover pipelines distort the underlying data distribution and yield spurious causal graphs. Second, identifying instantaneous effects is difficult even on complete data, and missingness further entangles imputation with graph recovery. Third, real-world data frequently exhibits heteroscedastic noise with variance driven by both instantaneous and lagged causes, violating the core assumptions of standard discovery methods. Existing approaches fail to address these challenges concurrently, typically presuming complete data, homoscedastic noise, or strictly time-lagged relationships. Crucially, we show through ablation studies that resolving these issues sequentially, rather than jointly, leads to a substantial degradation in performance. To overcome this, we introduce Cheesefill, an optimal transport framework for causal structure learning under missingness and heteroscedastic noise. Cheesefill parameterizes causal mechanisms using conditional normalizing flows and jointly learns a stochastic correction map that refines naive imputations into trajectories consistent with the inferred causal mechanisms. Theoretically, we prove that optimizing over stochastic correction maps is equivalent to a conditional kernel reformulation of the Kantorovich problem, from which our neural parameterization yields a tractable objective. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that Cheesefill consistently outperforms existing baselines across diverse missingness regimes.
entries.journalRef: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

entries.title: The Delta Gap: Cellular World Models for Perturbation Response Prediction Are Far Harder Than Global Correlation Implies
entries.abstract: Cellular world models aim to predict how cells respond to genetic perturbations, analogous to world models in reinforcement learning. Perturbation response models are evaluated almost exclusively by global Pearson correlation between predicted and observed transcriptomes. We show this metric is dominated by thousands of non-responsive genes and severely inflates apparent performance. On the Replogle K562 screen (509 unseen perturbations, 5000 genes), GEARS achieves global Pearson 0.977, but its delta Pearson is only 0.076. A trivial baseline predicting mean training delta achieves 0.267, which is 3.5x better than GEARS. Our primary contribution is methodological: we identify and quantify this delta gap as a systematic evaluation artifact, and propose delta-space evaluation as the primary benchmark. We provide two post-hoc corrections (RWR on co-expression graphs and kNN matching) and show that 2.8x of the remaining gap lies in perturbation representation geometry, not decoder capacity. We further show the gap is partially addressable end-to-end: delta-aligned training (lambda = 3.0) raises delta Pearson to 0.179 on Replogle (2.35x over GEARS) and surpasses the trivial baseline on direction accuracy (0.680 vs 0.567) and gene recovery (1.52 vs 1.19); combined with kNN it reaches 0.217. An amplitude-calibration variant (eta = 0.3) further raises gene recovery to 2.16 while reaching 0.218. Critically, these representations transfer zero-shot across cell lines: from Replogle K562 to unseen Norman A549, the delta-aligned model reaches 0.328 on 741 shared genes, 4.7x a trivial baseline and 2.1x standard GEARS. This is the first systematic quantification of the delta gap, and the first diagnostic framework localizing the residual gap to perturbation representation geometry via an oracle upper bound.

entries.title: STABLE: A Continual Learning Optimizer with Adaptive Drift Control
entries.abstract: Continual learning suffers from catastrophic forgetting, leading to the loss of past knowledge and unstable adaptation across task streams. Existing approaches typically address this issue through replay buffers, architectural changes, or additional regularization terms. We argue that forgetting is a consequence of unstable learning dynamics, which may benefit from an optimizer-level solution. The main challenge is that learning dynamics are time-dependent, as demonstrated by empirical phenomena such as the stability gap. First, we formally prove that, for distance-based classifiers, bounded parameter drift guarantees bounded margin erosion under a local score-stability condition. Based on this insight, we propose STABLE, a primal-dual optimizer with adaptive drift control. STABLE enforces a drift budget by increasing the dual variable when the budget is violated and decreasing it otherwise. This results in high stability without penalizing plasticity. Experiments on long-horizon unimodal streams and CLIP-based multimodal streams show that vanilla PEFT baselines trained with STABLE match or outperform specialized continual learning methods. In the multimodal setting, STABLE further preserves zero-shot transfer, matching or exceeding dedicated multimodal continual learning methods. Code is available at https://github.com/atlas-luiss/STABLE.
entries.comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

entries.title: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations
entries.abstract: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to each layer's activations, while absorbing the corresponding inverse transforms into its weights. Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve over round-to-nearest quantization, we introduce Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. Despite executing the activation transforms at inference time, MACaQ adds only 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. MACaQ reaches lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and already matches their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11 times less quantization time. We further apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, illustrating the generality of its layer-local design and show quantization of a 122B parameter model in 64 minutes, using only 32.5GB GPU RAM. Code is available at https://github.com/huawei-csl/MACaQ.

entries.title: On the Geometric Bottlenecks of Cross-Lingual Knowledge Editing
entries.abstract: Transformer-based autoregressive multilingual language models (LMs) are often assumed to store factual knowledge in an interlingua: a language-agnostic latent space. If this assumption holds, a parameter update applied in a source language during knowledge editing should inherently propagate to its semantic equivalents in target languages. However, empirical benchmarks show that cross-lingual propagation of edits often degrades substantially, a degradation that prior work treats largely as an algorithmic symptom rather than a structural bottleneck. In this work, we investigate whether representational anisotropy creates a structural bottleneck for source-only associative-memory editing, and perform a geometric dissection of the cross-lingual propagation gap. Using associative memory-based "locate-then-edit" methods, including ROME, MEMIT, and AlphaEdit, as analytical frameworks, we derive a closed-form decomposition of this gap into key-space propagation, parallel residual mismatch, and orthogonal residual mismatch. Our empirical findings show that cross-lingual propagation is primarily bottlenecked by a large orthogonal residual component, indicating that source-language edits often fail to span the target-language update directions required for successful transfer. Furthermore, we show that post-hoc correction using only source-language residual statistics encounters a large residual-prediction barrier. Finally, we perform a structural realignment via a targeted contrastive alignment objective and find that it substantially improves key-space propagation and partially improves cross-lingual edit transfer, while leaving value-space mismatch as a remaining bottleneck.

entries.title: SLA-Aware Task Offloading in the IoT Edge-Cloud Continuum: Class-Weighted Deep Reinforcement Learning Against an Exact Optimum
entries.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is often used to decide where Internet of Things (IoT) tasks with different latency limits run in the edge-cloud continuum, yet some methods give every missed task the same penalty and few compare their agents with an optimal policy. This benchmark study builds four offloading systems small enough to solve exactly by dynamic programming and measures reward and learner against the optimum. A bonus for a met limit makes each miss cost its penalty plus the bonus, which shifts the class weights of published per-class rewards. A class-blind penalty stays 65% to 118% above the optimal cost even with a perfect learner, while a corrected per-class penalty comes within 0.13% of the optimum. With a per-class reward, tuned proximal policy optimization (PPO) agents come within 9% to 11% of the optimum in the smallest system, and the corrected one beats a tuned reservation rule in 9 of 10 seeds. In larger systems the agents stay 41% to 76% above the optimum, and a tuned rule beats their mean. Training ten times longer does not close this gap, and a PPO-Lagrangian agent with reachable targets does no better than the per-class reward.

entries.title: Exploration via Exploitation: The Blessing of Reward Diversity in Personalized Federated RL
entries.abstract: While federated reinforcement learning (RL) has traditionally guaranteed high efficiency in homogeneous environments, collaboration is often hindered when agents possess distinct goals. In this paper, we flip this paradigm, framing reward heterogeneity not as a hurdle to consensus, but as a structural asset that catalyzes exploration. We first propose Personalized Federated Upper Confidence Bound Value Iteration (PF-UCBVI), which achieves optimal linear speedup by decoupling shared dynamics from personalized objectives. To eliminate the risks of explicit exploration, we then introduce Personalized Federated Exploration-Free Value Iteration (PF-EFVI), a purely greedy algorithm that leverages reward diversity to ensure state-action coverage. We prove that PF-EFVI attains logarithmic regret without explicit exploration bonuses under sufficient reward diversity. Our results reveal that agent disagreement shifts the exploration burden from temporal complexity to spatial diversity, enabling efficient collective learning without explicit exploration.

entries.title: Coverage-Verified Sparse Attention: Closed-Loop Quality Control for Long-Context LLM Decoding
entries.abstract: Sparse attention accelerates long-context decoding by reading a subset of the KV cache, but existing methods are open-loop: the kernel commits to its selection with no signal indicating whether enough attention mass was preserved and no recovery path when it was not. The needed signal already exists inside the kernel. The fraction of softmax mass on the selected tokens, which we call coverage, satisfies an exact algebraic equality with per-step output error and serves a dual role as the acceptance criterion and the interpolation weight for recovery. Coverage-Verified Sparse Attention (CVSA) turns coverage into a training-free, closed-loop verify-then-correct decode loop that accepts high-coverage drafts and recovers only the heads that fall short, with no sampling, no draft model, and no speculative-decoding infrastructure. Quality varies by only 0.14 points across the threshold sweep; budget and scheduling ablations characterize the deployed operating point. On LongBench at 7B and 70B, CVSA comes within 1.13 points of dense attention, statistically matching it at 70B, and it loses 0.8 points on RULER; measured median decode-step speedup reaches 6.21× at 128K context.
entries.comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 35 pages, 12 figures, 35 tables

entries.title: CONSTRAINER: Promptable Graph-Structured Optimization via Constraint Conditioning
entries.abstract: Neural methods for graph-structured optimization have achieved strong performance within individual problem classes, but are typically trained for fixed formulations, limiting reuse across related problem variants. Recent progress in foundation models has motivated shared neural backbones trained across multiple graph-structured optimization tasks; however, existing approaches primarily share instance-level representations while treating feasibility constraints implicitly. A key source of shared structure across constrained optimization problems is the constraint set itself, which often exhibits substantial overlap across tasks. We propose CONSTRAINER, a constraint-conditioned framework for graph-structured optimization that treats constraints as structured inputs. Constraint specifications are parsed into operator graphs and encoded using a graph neural network to produce invariant constraint embeddings, which condition a shared backbone model for solution prediction. We evaluate our approach on power grid optimization and mixed-integer linear programming problems, where it shows improved solution optimality and enables efficient transfer learning and generalization compared to baseline methods.

entries.title: What Do Collusion Probes Read? Three Pitfalls in Evaluating Multi-Agent Collusion Monitors
entries.abstract: Activation probes look like near-perfect monitors for secret collusion among large language model (LLM) agents. We show that they mostly detect that an agent was told to collude, not that it decided to. Our benchmark (2,500 committee and 1,476 code-review episodes) adds agents who receive the collusion instruction and refuse it, separating instruction from decision. Published detectors barely tell colluders from these refusers, and our best probe separates them mostly by reading the instruction: without it, agent AUROC falls from 1.00 to 0.61. Two further pitfalls inflate reported results: scored after the vote, a rule that only reads the votes reaches AUROC 0.990 but finds nothing before it; and in 57% of attempts no colluder argues for the target in public. The decision is still there: a probe trained on agents' own choices reads it (AUROC 0.73 without the instruction), and probes find colluders whose goal was fine-tuned into the weights (AUROC 0.995; pre-registered). We turn the controls into a protocol for testing any collusion monitor, and adapt scan statistics into an online monitor for groups of any size.
entries.comment: 30 pages, 5 figures. Code: https://github.com/mainul3195/collusion-probe-pitfalls ; data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/mainul3195/collusion-probe-pitfalls ; archive: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23636508

entries.title: NeuroHorizon: Long-Horizon Forecasting of Neural Population Activity with Hierarchical Memory
entries.abstract: Long-horizon forecasting of neural population activity tests whether a model has captured dynamics that remain predictive well beyond the observed history. Prediction quality typically declines as the horizon grows, yet neither short-horizon accuracy nor teacher-forced evaluation, which supplies the true activity preceding each predicted step, reveals how well models sustain predictions from an initial history alone. We compare direct multi-step prediction and autoregressive rollout on spiking recordings across horizons and introduce NeuroHorizon, which pairs event-based spike encoding with a causal decoder for population firing rates. Its hierarchical prediction memory keeps recent predictions at full temporal resolution and compresses earlier ones into segment summaries, giving the decoder both local detail and longer-range context. Under teacher-forced training this memory holds ground-truth activity, whereas during rollout it holds the model's own predictions. To reduce this mismatch, we train with scheduled sampling, progressively exposing the decoder to its own predictions. From 500 ms of macaque motor-cortex activity, NeuroHorizon achieves the highest forward-prediction score among the evaluated autonomous models at all four horizons from 100 to 1000 ms, and its per-bin predictions remain above a mean-firing-rate baseline across nearly the full 1 s window. Complementary experiments on macaque sensorimotor and mouse multi-region recordings show that performance generally increases with model and data size, alongside improved prediction after cross-subject pretraining and fine-tuning. Together, these results clarify how forecasting performance changes across horizons and offer an effective approach to long-horizon forecasting of neural population activity.
entries.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Main Track). 25 pages, including references, appendices, and the NeurIPS paper checklist

entries.title: Clinical Evidence-Guided Residual Learning for Medication Recommendation with Dynamic DDI Regularization
entries.abstract: Medication recommendation must combine patient-specific treatment evidence with the interaction structure of a prescription. The central challenge is to determine which evidence supports each medication and how strongly to regularize interactions while preserving predictive quality. We propose EviDrug, a clinical evidence-guided residual learning framework. Its clinical-memory backbone integrates a self-trained visit-aware encoder, training-case memory and one medication-set interaction block to establish a patient-specific prescription. A gated refinement head combines the backbone states with clinical associations and history-conditioned medication identities through bounded logit corrections. Drug-drug interaction (DDI) feedback adapts regularization strength using training-query predictions. Across MIMIC-IV, NWICU and SICdb, EviDrug leads twelve published-method baselines in AP, F1 and Jaccard, improving AP by 2.26, 2.06 and 1.71 percentage points over the strongest comparator. These gains come at lower parameter and runtime costs than MetaDrug. Matched controls demonstrate DDI reductions with stable predictive quality. Code is available at https://github.com/LIZESHENG13/EviDrug.
entries.comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. Supplementary PDF and detailed result tables are included as ancillary files. Code: https://github.com/LIZESHENG13/EviDrug

entries.title: Detent: Batch-Invariant LLM Serving and RL Rollouts at Near-Stock Speed
entries.abstract: Reproducible evaluation, verifiable inference and on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) need an LLM engine to give a request the same output bits whichever requests share its batch. Batch-invariant kernels exist, but engines still select each kernel and its parameters from the batch. Two kernels that compute the same sum can round it differently. The engines' deterministic modes remove the choice by keeping one conservative kernel per operator and pay for it in latency. Many fast kernels are batch-invariant by themselves, so it is enough to fix the few batch-dependent values that kernel selection reads. Detent expresses kernel selection as a program that the engine executes. It finds the fewest values in this program that must be fixed and tunes them for the workload before deployment. On multi-GPU deployments of Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-30B-A3B in vLLM and SGLang, Detent is batch-invariant. Tuned per load, it serves at 1.04-1.17x the latency per output token of Stock (each engine with its standard settings), against 1.67-10.3x for the deterministic modes. In SGLang it matches the GSM8K accuracy of SGLang's deterministic mode. Detent covers multiple deployment combinations, including multiple engines, GPU generations, tensor-parallel degrees, and dense and MoE models. Seeded RL rollouts of models up to Llama-3.1-70B replay bit for bit under other batches and cache splits. A trainer on Detent's kernels and values matches every rollout logprob bit for bit at 1.03x Stock's rollout time per token. BF16 GRPO then stays stable where Stock's run collapses.

entries.title: The RenAIssance: Caption-Guided Diffusion Models for Historical-Art Visual Media
entries.abstract: Generative AI can expand cultural collections into prompt-responsive visual media, but historical artworks rarely provide the paired descriptions needed to adapt modern image generators. We present The RenAIssance, a scalable pipeline that turns a collection of historical European artworks into a reusable text-to-image media resource. The pipeline generates scene-level captions with BLIP and uses the resulting approximately 15,000 image–text pairs from DEArt to train a compact LoRA adapter for Stable Diffusion v1.5. The adapter shifts generated images toward the historical-art distribution while retaining the base model's ability to render novel concepts. On historical and contemporary prompts of different lengths, it improves FID to the DEArt reference distribution in every setting with only a modest decrease in CLIP text–image similarity. Qualitative results show that the same adapter can render both period-appropriate subjects and contemporary concepts in a coherent historical visual language. By decoupling a reusable style representation from the base generator, the approach offers a practical building block for controllable historical-art media creation, interactive authoring, and rich-media experiences.
entries.comment: Accepted at ACMMM26 RichMediaGAI. This work is co-funded by the European Union's Horizon Europe research and innovation programme under MSCA with grant agreement No 101081674

entries.title: Predictive Modelling of Solid Waste Generation through Time Series Analysis
entries.abstract: Reliable forecasting of Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) production is pivotal for sustainable urban management, as it enables efficient resource planning, optimized collection schedules, and reduced environmental impacts. Existing works on MSW forecasting have some limitations, such as unavailability of granular data from lower administrative units, small datasets, limited or sometimes no consideration of important factors that can affect MSW generation, including holidays, weekends, seasonality, changes in temperature or humidity. This work presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of four popularly used time series forecasting models, namely Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average with Exogenous Regressors (SARIMAX), Prophet, Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), using a real-world MSW dataset from Sri Lanka spanning 2012-2018. A detailed factor-wise analysis is conducted to examine waste generation behaviour considering holidays, weekday-weekend variations, seasonal patterns, temperature and humidity. The results show lower waste generation during holidays and weekends, higher generation during Summer and Winter, and comparatively lower generation during Monsoon and Post-Monsoon. Temperature and humidity do not exhibit a direct linear relationship with waste generation, although their seasonal variations are associated with the changes in waste generation across different seasons. All model performances are evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), and the coefficient of determination (R2). Among the evaluated models, LSTM and SARIMAX achieve the best overall forecasting performance.

entries.title: Deep backward multistep high-order regression methods for high dimensional nonlinear parabolic partial differential equations
entries.abstract: We propose a deep backward multistep high-order regression (MHDBR) method for semilinear parabolic partial differential equations through their backward stochastic differential equation representations. The method combines multistep time discretization with regression targets formed by conditional expectations. Under explicit regularity, starting-value, forward-approximation and network-moment assumptions, we prove an error bound separating time discretization, conditional Monte Carlo sampling and neural-network approximation. The analysis assumes exact population minimization; finite-training-sample generalization and optimization errors are not included. For generators independent of the gradient variable, suitably constrained GroupSort networks and sufficiently large conditional sample sizes give order J in the stated nodal L² error norm. The required network sizes depend on dimension, so this result does not establish dimension-independent complexity. We present a reproducible time-discretization test satisfying the analytical assumptions and three broader neural-network benchmarks, whose relation to the assumptions is discussed explicitly.

entries.title: Confronting Uncertainty in Mechanism-AI Coupled Dynamical Systems via Optimal Transport and Information Geometry: Part I. Distribution Learning
entries.abstract: Mechanism-AI coupled dynamical systems are increasingly used to study complex biological systems. However, uncertainty associated with noisy, sparse, and partially observed data limits their reliability. This paper presents a systematic mathematical formulation for treating these uncertainties from the perspective of optimal transport and information geometry. We formulate the uncertainty quantification problem as the minimization of an energy functional on a probability density space equipped with a Riemannian metric, with the loss evaluated through a differential equation, and give a unified description of the gradient flows of the energy functional under specific metrics, such as the Wasserstein and Fisher-Rao metrics. Furthermore, we present corresponding numerical methods for solving these gradient flows using abstract adjoint sensitivity analysis. The formulation connects a range of Bayesian inference methods for dynamical systems; numerical experiments compare posterior approximation and predictive uncertainty under a common computational budget. Moreover, it also provides a geometric perspective on dynamical modeling and the study of heterogeneity evolution.

entries.title: Large Language Models without QK-Normalization
entries.abstract: Query-Key Normalization (QK-Norm) is widely adopted in modern large language models to control the growth of attention logits and improve training stability. However, query and key norms are not merely sources of instability. The query norm controls the sharpness of the attention distribution, while the key norm determines how strongly a token attracts different queries. These norms therefore carry token-specific information about attention selectivity and token importance. By normalizing both, QK-Norm suppresses this information. This raises a natural question: can we control query-key representations without discarding their sensitivity to magnitude? To address this question, we propose QK-MAP, a Magnitude-Aware Projection for constructing queries and keys. Rather than removing magnitude through normalization, QK-MAP transforms the input representation using multiple learnable frequencies, so that changes in magnitude are encoded as bounded phase patterns. This allows magnitude to be represented through phase and direction rather than vector length alone. Its periodic features have a fixed norm while remaining sensitive to magnitude changes, separating magnitude encoding from norm growth. Multiple frequencies further help distinguish magnitudes and reduce periodic ambiguity. Experiments across model scales from 190M to 7B parameters show that QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss than both Standard attention and QK-Norm. Further analyses show that QK-MAP preserves sensitivity to input scale, assigns less attention to the first token, and produces stronger attention contrast for relevant evidence in synthetic long-context tests. These results demonstrate that query-key scale can be effectively controlled without sacrificing token-specific magnitude information.

entries.title: onóna: Twin Embeddings with Tied Unembeddings
entries.abstract: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate onóna across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.

entries.title: Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning
entries.abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) trains agents to adapt to novel tasks from test-time experience, but requires diverse training environments and reward functions. While environments are becoming cheaper to generate, it remains difficult to anticipate every objective an agent may be asked to pursue at test time. Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) learn policies from reward-free data and support zero-shot RL (ZSRL): adaptation to new objectives at test time using a large reward-labeled dataset. Recent work has shown that BFM task inference can instead be performed online without prior task-specific data. We note that this capability positions BFMs and meta-RL as alternative approaches for online adaptation to new reward functions in a fixed environment. We then ask whether we can extend BFMs to compete with meta-RL more broadly, including in novel environments, and identify four challenges: environment identification, online data collection, test-time exploration, and learning from mixed reward supervision. We study each individually, then propose MetaBFM, a hybrid method that addresses all four. During training, it combines supervised reward-following with unsupervised learning; at test time, it can interpolate between exploration, exploitation, and ZSRL-style reward inference. We demonstrate that MetaBFM can recover the in-distribution performance of supervised meta-RL while generalizing to reward functions outside the training set. Our work suggests that BFMs and meta-RL are complementary research directions whose combined strengths allow adaptive agents to learn more diverse behaviors from a fixed set of supervised objectives.

entries.title: Seeing Isn't Enough: Unlocking Visual Reasoning by Bridging the Reasoning-Access Gap with TIGER
entries.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) inherit strong textual reasoning capabilities from their language backbones and text pretraining, but often fail to apply the same level of competency to visual inputs. We show that this degradation cannot be attributed to only perception failures, by evaluating models on semantically-equivalent text and rendered-text image inputs: models can accurately read text in the images and recover near-text performance when provided their own transcriptions, but just cannot reason well on the images directly. We characterize this discrepancy as a modality reasoning-access gap, where models fail to route perceived visual content into existing reasoning machinery accessible with text. To bridge this, we propose TIGER (Text-to-Image Gap-targeted training for Enhanced Reasoning), which first mines synthetic modality counterfactuals where a model succeeds on a text problem but fails when provided the corresponding rendered image, and post-trains the model on the image input via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), along with SFT and DPO variants. Importantly, although trained exclusively on synthetic rendered-text images with no multimodal annotations, TIGER results in model performance improvements across diverse real-world visual benchmarks including geometric diagrams (MathVerse), multi-disciplinary sciences (EMMA, MMMU), complex charts (ChartQAPro), and embodied spatial reasoning (RoboSpatial-Home). TIGER also complements existing state-of-the-art RLVR visual reasoning methods, yielding further performance gains. Analysis involving reasoning-subspace activation and activation patching provide support indicating that TIGER helps to align visual-to-reasoning pathways toward text reasoning states. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/minhngh/Tiger.
entries.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Gregory and Minh contributed equally

entries.title: Dual-Granularity Learning for Regression with Continuous Noisy Labels
entries.abstract: Learning with noisy labels has been extensively studied for classification, yet its regression counterpart remains relatively underexplored. Unlike classification, regression involves continuous-valued targets where label noise exhibits heterogeneous magnitudes across instances, which poses conflicting requirements on the model: correcting small-to-moderate deviations requires sensitivity to label values for instance-level refinement, whereas large deviations caused by corrupted or outlying annotations render exact label values unreliable, necessitating reduced reliance on exact labels and instead leveraging ordinal structure among samples. These requirements call for methods that capture both global structure and sample-specific deviations in a unified manner. To this end, we propose GRAIN, a dual-granularity framework for robust noisy regression. At the fine-grained level, we derive an explicit residual learning mechanism from a robust loss formulation, introducing instance-specific auxiliary variables to decouple label noise from predictive signals. At the coarse-grained level, we introduce a binning-based contrastive regularization that enforces an order-preserving feature structure aligned with label proximity, addressing noise beyond the capacity of local residual refinement. The two levels are coupled via a histogram-based bridging mechanism that enables bidirectional information flow: coarse-grained structural guidance establishes a well-ordered feature space that anchors residual learning, while fine-grained residual refinement corrects instance-level deviations that structural regularization alone cannot resolve. Experimental results show that GRAIN consistently improves robustness and generalization under diverse noise conditions.

entries.title: Compact Quantum Channel Attention for Static ASL Recognition: A Controlled Study with Parameter-Matched Baselines
entries.abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical models often report good accuracy on image tasks, but it is rarely clear whether the quantum part is responsible. This paper proposes QCA-DenseNet, a static American Sign Language (ASL) recognition pipeline in which an eight-qubit variational circuit acts as a channel-attention gate on DenseNet121 features. The quantum channel attention (QCA) gate has 17,464 parameters, 7.51 times fewer than a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) block. The pipeline is tested on 1,815 MU HandImages images by holding out one of five signers at a time, and a frozen-backbone ablation uses small parts of the Kaggle ASL Alphabet data. On unseen signers, QCA-DenseNet reaches 94.50% mean accuracy, above SE (93.72%) and within 0.28 points of the best model. A matched classical MLP and a model without attention perform about the same, and no difference is significant. QCA gives a much smaller attention gate without a detectable loss in accuracy, but no quantum advantage.

entries.title: Intra-Option Fitted Q-Evaluation: Evaluating Hierarchical Policies from Non-Hierarchical Data
entries.abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the expected return of a target policy from previously collected data without additional environment interaction. While OPE methods for flat Markovian policies are well studied, little work has addressed evaluating hierarchical policies in which a high-level policy selects temporally extended options that generate primitive actions until a termination condition is met. The primary existing approach applies per-decision importance sampling at the option level, but requires option-annotated trajectories and exhibits variance that still grows with the horizon. For non-hierarchical policies, fitted Q-evaluation (FQE) typically achieves lower error than importance sampling by leveraging the classic Bellman equation for policy evaluation; however, a naive extension of FQE to hierarchical policies results in a biased policy value estimate. In this paper, we introduce Intra-Option Fitted Q-Evaluation (IO-FQE), which estimates a value function in the augmented state-option space; this approach enables OPE of hierarchical policies even when we lack annotations of what option was run in the data. We develop two continuous-action instantiations of IO-FQE and show on long-horizon hierarchical continuous control tasks (AntMaze navigation and OGBench Puzzle manipulation) that IO-FQE eliminates the bias incurred by a naive application of FQE to hierarchical policies and substantially lowers mean squared-error compared to option-level importance sampling.

entries.title: Close and Sort: Exact Maximum-Likelihood Aggregation of Cyclic Rank-Two Preferences
entries.abstract: Pairwise probabilities arise in rank aggregation, recommendation, and human or LLM evaluation, yet converting them into a maximum-likelihood list is a weighted Kemeny problem and is NP-hard in general. Known exact algorithms for rank-two tournaments use only comparison signs and do not optimize this likelihood. We show that the weighted problem is exactly solvable when the skew-symmetric log-odds matrix W_(ij)=log(p_(ij)/p_(ji)) has rank two, including when the induced preferences contain cycles. Writing W_(ij)=det(h_i,h_j) and adding the closing vector h₀=-Σ_i h_i turns the objective into twice the signed area of a closed polygon. This geometry yields CloseSort, which polar-sorts the n+1 edge vectors, cuts after h₀, and returns a global maximum-likelihood order in O(nlogn) time from the factors. The same geometry identifies the runner-up and gives a stability certificate beyond exact rank two. When the smallest determinant δ of two consecutive edges in the closed angular cycle is positive, it is exactly the best-to-runner-up log-likelihood gap. For W=W₀+E, the CloseSort order of W₀ has regret at most Σ_(i<j)|E_(ij)| on W and remains optimal whenever this sum is below δ, a worst-case tight threshold. In 5,120 determinant-logit simulations, increasing the observations per pair from 4 to 64 raises the fraction on which rank-two projection outperforms the empirical plug-in optimum from 68.6% to 85.7%. On 3,600 Arena-Hard LLM-judge profiles drawn from 63 systems and ten judges, the leading rank-two component captures 89.2% of the log-odds energy. On profiles containing a directed majority triangle, CloseSort reduces normalized regret by 44% relative to Borda and improves the mean normalized objective over each of eight baselines. With factors supplied, it is 8,407 times faster than exact dynamic programming on 18-item rankings.
entries.comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the 20th ACM International Conference on Web Search and Data Mining (WSDM 2027). Code: https://github.com/sarinstein-yan/close-and-sort

entries.title: In Search of Lost Time: Temporal Competence in Large Language Models
entries.abstract: Today's large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact with time: AI agents schedule tasks, coordinate with people and other AI systems, and even decide how long to think. Yet LLMs only ever encounter time secondhand—in descriptions rather than experience. Does this hinder their reasoning and decisions that involve time? Our paper traces this question from a model's knowledge to its actions through four successive evaluations. We find that models know the rules of time, which can be read, but struggle to predict durations, which must be lived; while they are highly accurate (92.0-97.5%) on a collection of questions built from the theorems of various time-related literatures, they underestimate their own completion times by up to 99.5% and fail to identify which tasks will take them longer to run. And while they are better at estimating durations of human tasks, their duration judgments change based on how an event is worded, magnifying similar human biases by up to 1.3×. Moving from estimation to action, we find that some LLMs disregard time costs completely when answering user queries, ignoring a 1,200-fold increase in wait time entirely. Together, our experiments reveal new challenges posed to LLMs as they navigate a dimension they cannot directly perceive, and highlight how their blind spots can even be simple cognitive abilities that humans take for granted.

entries.title: Action Transfer Across Character Body Plans in Latent-Action World Models: An Empirical Study of Animated Characters
entries.abstract: Latent-action world models learn actions from video without labels, and recent methods aim to share these actions across bodies. Transfer between 2D characters with different body structures remains underexplored. In this paper, we study whether an action learned from one character can make a character with a different body perform the same action. A cat, a blob and a human can all jump, but each moves its body in its own way. The usual transfer gain mixes body motion with screen movement and can assign a perfect score to a model that ignores its action. To address this, we introduce a transfer score that compares the correct action with wrong ones from the same source. We test five training objectives on a new synthetic benchmark of 2D cartoon characters with six body plans, the standard Sprites benchmark, and 431 selected animal and human animations from DeformingThings4D. With a fixed camera, a baseline that only copies the source's screen movement scores 0.71, as high as most learned models. In contrast, with a camera that follows the body, the best model reaches only 0.46 for an unseen animal family and 0.20 for humans. With this camera, a linear probe identifies the action class of unseen animal families with 66% to 86% balanced accuracy (chance 17%). The learned actions therefore retain information about which action is performed, but the correct action closes only part of the prediction error gap for a new character.

entries.title: TimeHF 2.0: Multimodal, Multivariate, and Multi-Region Collaborative Forecasting for Large-Scale Retail Supply Chains
entries.abstract: Large-scale retail supply chains need sales forecasts for specified products, future dates or planning windows, and regions under the conditions available at the forecast origin. Regional sparsity, changing environments, volatile sales, and unfamiliar business situations make these dimensions difficult to model together. We introduce TimeHF 2.0, a multimodal, multivariate, and multi-region collaborative forecasting framework that makes flexibly expressed business knowledge usable in numerical prediction. A coverage-aware directed encoder integrates regional sales and applicable covariates. A semantic alignment module transfers language-model hidden representations of natural-language plans and domain experience into target-specific forecasting context. Learning against sales observations connects these meanings to numerical evidence, allowing business users to supply experience, future plans, and changing circumstances without defining a new numerical feature for each description. Text-conditioned future queries and shared/routed experts adapt prediction to the supplied context. An ordered-distribution head allocates fine resolution to routine fluctuations and coarse resolution to extreme sales movements, while daily/window learning connects forecasts to cumulative planning quantities. Online parallel forecasting at JD yields relative accuracy improvements of 18.25% and 17.94% for national daily and planning-window sales, and 19.44% and 18.99% for DC daily and planning-window sales, over the original production deep learning baseline. Component comparisons, loss-design results, and product-type analyses examine the roles of regional information, covariates, business knowledge, context-dependent processing, and robust planning-oriented learning.

entries.title: ADIndex: Layer-Adaptive Sparse Attention Indexing via Group-Level Distillation
entries.abstract: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) reduces the computational cost of attention through token-level selection. However, its indexer still scores the entire causal prefix for each query, making indexing a dominant source of latency in long-context inference. Notably, the indexer alone can account for more than 50% of total prefill GPU time at long context lengths. To address this bottleneck, we propose ADIndex, an Adaptive and Distillation-driven Indexing method for token-level sparse attention. ADIndex integrates three key components: (i) a layer-wise calibration strategy that adaptively accommodates cross-query retrieval overlap, motivated by our observation of pronounced inter-layer heterogeneity; (ii) a group-level distillation scheme that leverages this heterogeneity to efficiently train adaptive layer-wise group indexers, capturing salient retrieval signals from individual queries; and (iii) a low-latency inference strategy that reduces repeated full-prefix scans through token bank sharing within query groups while retaining query-specific refinement. Experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1 demonstrate that ADIndex preserves near-lossless task performance on LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER while delivering substantial efficiency gains over standard DSA, including prefill and decoding kernel speedups of up to 6.22x and 3.40x, respectively, at a context length of 256K across the layer-wise reuse configurations, as well as an end-to-end serving speedup of 1.54x at a context length of 128K.

entries.title: FADE: Fractional Anomalous Dynamics Extrapolation for Training-Free Diffusion Transformers Acceleration
entries.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have established themselves as the preeminent paradigm for high-fidelity generative modeling across various modalities, yet their practical deployment is hindered by the severe computational overhead of iterative sampling. While recent feature-caching methods mitigate this latency through feature reuse or forecasting based on integer-order operators, they remain limited in adapting to the non-stationary and highly curved dynamics of DiT latent trajectories. In this work, we reveal that DiT feature evolution exhibits anomalous diffusion characteristics and a certain degree of spatiotemporal heterogeneity, rendering static, integer-order forecasting operators inadequate and prone to error accumulation. To address this, we propose Fractional Anomalous Dynamics Extrapolation (FADE), a unified framework for training-free diffusion transformers acceleration. FADE models DiT feature evolution via anomalous diffusion and employs a Mittag–Leffler fractional operator to better adapt to high-curvature and non-linear latent trajectories of DiTs. Leveraging the empirical observation that these complex dynamics maintain cross-sample stability, we further construct a Look-Up Table with multiple dimensions through offline profiling. This enables negligible LUT-retrieval overhead, spatiotemporally adaptive parameter retrieval during online inference. Extensive evaluations across diverse architectures and modalities demonstrate that FADE achieves state-of-the-art acceleration, preserving exceptional generation fidelity under aggressive skip intervals with negligible latency overhead. Our project page is available at https://youngkinlon.github.io/fade-project-page/.

entries.title: CALFA-KV: Joint Calibration and Fisher-Guided Anchors for 1-Bit KV Cache Compression
entries.abstract: 1-bit key-value (KV) cache compression can combine quantizer calibration with selective high-precision storage to reduce reconstruction error. We propose Calibration and Fisher-guided Anchors for KV cache compression (CALFA-KV). Offline, we jointly fit a key center, radial normalization parameters, and K/V vector codebooks to match the frozen model's projected attention output. We also estimate channel-wise Fisher-type sensitivities from squared gradients of a reference next-token cross-entropy loss. Online, we use these sensitivities to weight the squared reconstruction errors of each KV state. Here, a KV state is one token's key-value pair within one layer and KV head. We retain the highest-scoring states at high precision under a per-layer, per-KV-head budget. Under exact restoration, we bound the excess risk of score-based anchor selection relative to the optimum at the same anchor budget, where risk is the conditional mean square of the first-order loss change. With a budget of 56 additional FP16 anchors per layer and KV head, CALFA-KV (d8b8) outperforms all evaluated nominal 1-bit baselines on the mean score across seven benchmarks for each of the three models. At the same anchor budget, CALFA-KV (d8b10) uses a nominal index rate of 1.25 bits per channel and narrows the gap to BF16 to 0.90–2.01 points on the same metric.

entries.title: Predictive Surprise as Self-Grounding Concept Bottleneck for Interpretable Time Series
entries.abstract: Time-series classifiers deployed in risk-sensitive domains must be (1) accurate, (2) interpretable, and (3) able to abstain when evidence is weak. Existing methods do not deliver all 3 at once, and the obstacle is structural, rather than logistical. Meaningful temporal patterns cannot be defined without knowing segment boundaries, yet meaningful boundaries cannot be placed without knowing which patterns to expect.
